children.title: Original-Space Hull Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Hull descriptions expressed without auxiliary lifting variables.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-Optimization Characterization of the Closed Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-value test for closed-hull exactness in the original variable space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, with \(C\) closed and convex. Then \[C=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\] if and only if, for every \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\inf_{x\in C}c^\top x=\inf_{s\in S}c^\top s,\] where the values may be extended-real.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex original-space relaxation is the closed convex hull exactly when every linear objective has the same infimum over the relaxation and the original set.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) are nonempty.
\(C\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\iff \inf_C c^\top x=\inf_S c^\top x\) for every \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Optimization Characterization of the Closed Hull

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between finite linear hull descriptions and nonpolyhedral closed hulls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). There exist a finite matrix \(A\) and vector \(b\) such that \[C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\] if and only if \(C\) is a polyhedron. Consequently, a nonpolyhedral closed convex hull has no finite description consisting only of linear inequalities in the original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex hull has a finite original-space linear inequality description exactly when it is polyhedral.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty.
\(C=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\{x:Ax\le b\}\) for finite \((A,b)\) if and only if \(C\) is polyhedral.

notation.meaning: closed convex hull of the original set

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Linear Original-Space Description Criterion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Valid-Halfspace Representation of the Closed Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Original-space representation by all affine inequalities valid for the source set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)=\bigcap\left\{\{x:a^\top x\le\beta\}:a^\top s\le\beta\text{ for every }s\in S\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed convex hull is the intersection of all closed halfspaces containing the original set.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\) equals the intersection of all closed halfspaces containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.title: Valid-Halfspace Representation of the Closed Convex Hull

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H=\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional descriptions involving only the original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An original-space hull description of \(S\) is a system of equalities and inequalities in \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), with feasible region \(H\), such that \(H=\operatorname{conv}(S)\). If closed convex feasible regions are required, the corresponding target is \(H=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\). No auxiliary variable is permitted in the defining system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An original-space hull description uses only the original variables and defines exactly the convex hull, or its closure when closed feasible regions are required.
knowledge_statements.title: Original-Space Hull Descriptions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the original-space hull container, but the record supplies no evidence for the terminology or closure convention.

children.title: Extended Hull Formulations
children.top_down_role: Hull descriptions using auxiliary variables, disaggregation, or higher-dimensional convex sets.

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty.
\(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex-hull representations in a higher-dimensional space.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An extended hull formulation of \(S\) is a convex set \(Q=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+p}:F(x,y)\leq 0,\ G(x,y)=0\}\) whose original-variable projection satisfies \[\operatorname{proj}_x(Q):=\{x:\exists y,\ (x,y)\in Q\}=\operatorname{conv}(S).\] The variables \(y\) may encode disaggregation, conic lifts, or other auxiliary structure without changing the represented original-space hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended hull formulation is a convex lifted system whose projection onto the original variables equals the convex hull of the original feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended Hull Formulations

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary explaining why the bounded disaggregated formulation cannot be applied unchanged to arbitrary unbounded disjuncts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For unbounded polyhedra, constraints \(A_i x^i\le b_i\lambda_i\) permit \(x^i\in\operatorname{rec}P_i\) when \(\lambda_i=0\). These zero-weight recession contributions can describe points in the closure of the disjunctive hull that are absent from the hull itself. Thus boundedness, or an additional recession-compatible formulation theorem, is needed before asserting exact equality with an unclosed hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an unbounded disjunction, zero-weight blocks can carry recession directions, so the bounded disaggregated formula may represent only a closed or enlarged hull without further hypotheses.
assumptions_latex: At least one disjunct \(P_i=\{x:A_i x\le b_i\}\) is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_i=0\) allows \(x^i\in\operatorname{rec}P_i\); exactness for \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iP_i)\) therefore requires additional recession analysis.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Weight Recession Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Disaggregated Hull Formulation for a Finite Union of Polytopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical auxiliary-variable hull formulation for a bounded finite disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A_i x\le b_i\}\) be nonempty polytopes for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Then \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iP_i)\) is the projection of \[x=\sum_{i=1}^m x^i,\qquad A_i x^i\le b_i\lambda_i,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1,\qquad \lambda_i\ge0.\] Because each \(P_i\) is bounded, \(A_i x^i\le0\) forces \(x^i=0\), so zero-weight blocks introduce no recession points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite union of polytopes has an exact disaggregated extended hull formulation using one scaled copy and one weight per disjunct.
assumptions_latex: \(P_i=\{x:A_i x\le b_i\}\) is a nonempty polytope for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed lifted polyhedron projects onto \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_{i=1}^mP_i)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Disaggregated Hull Formulation for a Finite Union of Polytopes

children.title: Lifted-Space Projection
children.top_down_role: Recovery of original-variable relaxation geometry from extended formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifted-Space Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate projection of finite-dimensional convex lifted sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty convex set \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\), its original-variable projection is \[P=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^p,\ (x,y)\in Q\}.\] The projected set \(P\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The original-coordinate projection of a nonempty convex lifted set is the convex set obtained by existentially quantifying its auxiliary variables.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) is a nonempty convex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^p,\ (x,y)\in Q\}\) is convex.

notation.meaning: coordinate projection onto the original variables

source_refs.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological boundary for finite-dimensional convex lifted sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \[Q=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y\ge1/x\}\] is nonempty, closed, and convex, but \[\operatorname{proj}_xQ=(0,\infty)\] is not closed. By contrast, a coordinate projection of a compact set is compact, and a coordinate projection of a polyhedron is a polyhedron; hence both are closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-dimensional projection preserves convexity but not closedness; compactness or polyhedrality gives standard sufficient closedness regimes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\) is closed and convex while \(\operatorname{proj}_xQ=(0,\infty)\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Need Not Preserve Closedness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-interior geometry of finite-dimensional convex projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\) is nonempty and convex, then \[\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{proj}_xQ)=\operatorname{proj}_x(\operatorname{ri}Q).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty finite-dimensional convex set, projecting its relative interior gives the relative interior of its projection.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\) is nonempty and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{proj}_xQ)=\operatorname{proj}_x(\operatorname{ri}Q)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Relative Interior Commutes with Projection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual representation of a coordinate projection through the support function of the lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any nonempty \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\), with \(P=\operatorname{proj}_xQ\), \[\sigma_P(u)=\sup_{x\in P}\langle u,x\rangle=\sup_{(x,y)\in Q}\langle(u,0),(x,y)\rangle=\sigma_Q(u,0).\] Thus every linear objective involving only original variables has the same supremum over the lift and its projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function of a projection is the lifted support function evaluated with zero coefficients on auxiliary variables.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\) is nonempty.
\(P=\operatorname{proj}_xQ\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_P(u)=\sigma_Q(u,0)\) for every \(u\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.title: Support Function under Projection

children.title: Auxiliary-Variable Elimination
children.top_down_role: Removal of lifted variables while preserving relevant relaxation information.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact elimination of auxiliary variables determined by affine equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a lifted system contains \(Ey=Fx+g\) with \(E\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}\) nonsingular, substituting \[y=E^{-1}(Fx+g)\] into every remaining constraint eliminates \(y\) exactly. More generally, row reduction identifies pivot auxiliary variables for substitution, while free auxiliary variables remain for subsequent elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invertible affine equalities permit exact auxiliary-variable elimination by solving and substituting.
assumptions_latex: The equality coefficient matrix for the eliminated auxiliary block is nonsingular, or row reduction identifies a nonsingular pivot block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Substitution produces a system with exactly the same original-variable projection.

notation.meaning: coefficient matrix of the eliminated auxiliary block

knowledge_statements.title: Equality Elimination by Substitution

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual inequality description of a polyhedral projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[Q=\{(x,y):Ax+By\le d\},\] one has \[x\in\operatorname{proj}_xQ\iff \lambda^TAx\le\lambda^Td\quad\text{for every }\lambda\ge0\text{ satisfying }B^T\lambda=0.\] The cone \(\{\lambda\ge0:B^T\lambda=0\}\) is polyhedral and pointed, so a finite extreme-ray generating set suffices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative Farkas multipliers that cancel the auxiliary columns give an exact inequality description of a polyhedral projection.
assumptions_latex: \(Q=\{(x,y):Ax+By\le d\}\) is a finite-dimensional polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_xQ=\{x:\lambda^TAx\le\lambda^Td\ \forall\lambda\ge0,\ B^T\lambda=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Farkas Elimination Description

assumptions_latex: \(Q=\{(x,y):Ax+By\leq d\}\) is a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\{x:Cx\leq e\}\) for the inequalities remaining after elimination.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fourier–Motzkin elimination for polyhedral lifts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: To eliminate one component \(y_j\), normalize every inequality containing it as \(y_j\leq u_i(x,y_{-j})\) or \(y_j\geq \ell_k(x,y_{-j})\). Replace those inequalities by all pairwise conditions \(\ell_k(x,y_{-j})\leq u_i(x,y_{-j})\), retain inequalities independent of \(y_j\), and discard the eliminated inequalities. Repeat for every auxiliary component. Remove redundant inequalities if desired; the final system \(Cx\leq e\) defines \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fourier–Motzkin elimination removes each auxiliary variable by pairing its lower and upper bounds; the remaining inequalities describe the exact polyhedral projection.
knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Variable Elimination

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm correctly describes Fourier–Motzkin elimination for an inequality-form polyhedron and fits the elimination leaf, but no inspectable source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Projection Complexity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Representation growth or structural loss arising during projection.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial output bound for eliminating one scalar auxiliary variable from a linear inequality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(m\) inequalities \(a_i y+b_i^Tx\le c_i\), partitioned into \(P=\{i:a_i>0\}\), \(N=\{i:a_i<0\}\), and \(Z=\{i:a_i=0\}\). Fourier–Motzkin elimination of \(y\) retains the \(|Z|\) zero-coefficient inequalities and generates one inequality for every pair in \(P\times N\). Before redundancy removal, the projected description therefore contains at most \[|P||N|+|Z|\] inequalities, so a single elimination step can have quadratic output growth and repeated steps can compound that growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating one variable pairs every positive-coefficient inequality with every negative-coefficient inequality, producing potentially quadratic growth before redundancy removal.
assumptions_latex: The lifted system consists of finitely many linear inequalities.
One scalar variable is eliminated by Fourier–Motzkin elimination.
Duplicate and redundant inequalities are counted before removal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: m_{\mathrm{out}}\le |P||N|+|Z|,\quad\text{with }|P||N|=\Theta(m^2)\text{ possible}.

notation.meaning: positive, negative, and zero coefficient index sets for the eliminated variable
number of generated or retained inequalities before redundancy removal

knowledge_statements.title: One-Step Fourier–Motzkin Inequality Growth

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Permutahedra Separate Lift Size from Facet Count
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete polyhedral family exhibiting exponentially fewer lifted inequalities than original-space facets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge3\), let \[\Pi_n=\operatorname{conv}\{(\sigma(1),\ldots,\sigma(n)):\sigma\in S_n\}.\] In its affine hull \(\sum_i x_i=n(n+1)/2\), \(\Pi_n\) has one facet for each nonempty proper subset of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), hence \(2^n-2\) facets. Sorting-network constructions give exact extended linear formulations projecting to \(\Pi_n\) with \(O(n\log n)\) inequalities. Thus original-space facet count can be exponential while an exact lifted description is polynomial in \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The permutahedron has exponentially many original-space facets but admits a polynomial-size sorting-network lift.
assumptions_latex: Size counts linear inequalities; affine equations are recorded separately or converted under a fixed counting convention.
Extended formulations may introduce auxiliary variables and are compared by exact projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(\Pi_n)=2^n-2,\qquad \operatorname{xc}(\Pi_n)=O(n\log n).

notation.meaning: number of facets relative to the affine hull
minimum inequality count of an exact polyhedral extension

knowledge_statements.title: Permutahedra Separate Lift Size from Facet Count

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slack-matrix characterization of polyhedral extension complexity under an inequality-count convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a nonempty polytope of positive dimension, let \(S\) be a slack matrix formed from a facet description and the vertices of \(P\), and count only inequalities in an extended formulation while allowing affine equations at no cost. Then \[\operatorname{xc}(P)=\operatorname{rank}_+(S),\] where \(\operatorname{rank}_+(S)\) is the least \(r\) for which \(S=TU\) with \(T\in\mathbb R_+^{f\times r}\) and \(U\in\mathbb R_+^{r\times v}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polytope's minimum number of inequalities in an exact linear lift equals the nonnegative rank of its slack matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty positive-dimensional polytope.
\(S\) is a vertex-facet slack matrix of \(P\).
Extension size counts inequalities and treats affine equations as free.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{xc}(P)=\operatorname{rank}_+(S).

notation.meaning: Vertex-facet slack matrix of the polytope.
Nonnegative rank of the slack matrix.
Minimum inequality count of an exact polyhedral extension of \(P\).

knowledge_statements.title: Yannakakis Factorization Theorem

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Correlation Polytopes Have Exponential Extension Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A polyhedral family showing that auxiliary variables cannot always yield polynomial-size exact linear formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge 1\), define the correlation polytope \[\operatorname{COR}(n)=\operatorname{conv}\{xx^\top:x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\subseteq\mathbb S^n.\] Under the convention that extension size counts linear inequalities and permits affine equations at no cost, there exists a constant \(c>0\) such that \[\operatorname{xc}(\operatorname{COR}(n))\ge 2^{cn}\] for all sufficiently large \(n\). Consequently, every exact polyhedral lift of this family has exponentially many inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Correlation polytopes require exponentially large exact linear extended formulations, so lifting does not universally produce compact descriptions.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{COR}(n)\) is represented as a polytope in the symmetric-matrix coordinate space.
Extension size counts inequalities and treats affine equations as free.
Only exact polyhedral extended formulations are considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{xc}(\operatorname{COR}(n))=2^{\Omega(n)}.

notation.meaning: Correlation polytope generated by binary rank-one matrices.
Minimum inequality count of an exact polyhedral extension of a polytope.

knowledge_statements.title: Correlation Polytopes Have Exponential Extension Complexity

assumptions_latex: \(Q\) ranges over polyhedral extended formulations.
Size means the number of linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}(P)\) need not be polynomially related to the number of facets in an original-space description of \(P\).

notation.meaning: minimum size of a polyhedral extension projecting to the polytope

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral description size under projection and elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Projection preserves convexity but not description size. Define \(\operatorname{xc}(P)\) as the minimum number of inequalities in any polyhedron \(Q\) satisfying \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=P\). Eliminating auxiliary variables from a small \(Q\) can generate exponentially many intermediate or irredundant original-space inequalities. Consequently, a polynomial-size lifted description does not imply a polynomial-size original-space facet description, and explicit elimination need not be computationally economical.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small lifted formulation can project to a polytope requiring many original-space inequalities, while explicit elimination may incur exponential growth.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Complexity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The qualitative boundary is plausible, but the claimed exponential separation and the conclusion's phrase “need not be polynomially related” require a precise complexity theorem and a sourced separating family.

children.title: Ideal Formulation Principle
children.top_down_role: Ideality and exactness organized according to the space in which the relaxation is assessed.

children.title: Ideality in Original-Variable Projection
children.top_down_role: Ideality assessed after eliminating auxiliary variables.

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is the original feasible set.
\(R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) is a convex relaxation containing a lift of every point of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection-level ideality, allowing nonunique or nonintegral lifts.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relaxation \(R\) is ideal in original-variable projection when \[\operatorname{proj}_x(R)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S).\] If \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is closed, the closure may be omitted. This condition concerns only attainable original vectors: fibers \(\{y:(x,y)\in R\}\) may contain fractional or otherwise nonstructural auxiliary points without violating projection ideality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted relaxation is projection-ideal when eliminating its auxiliaries gives exactly the closed convex hull of the original feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Ideality in Original-Variable Projection

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection Ideality Does Not Control Auxiliary Fibers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of conclusions about lifted witnesses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The equality \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\) does not require a fiber \(R_x=\{y:(x,y)\in R\}\) to be a singleton, bounded, integral, or equal to the convex hull of the intended witnesses. Thus projection ideality alone does not certify extended-space ideality or recovery of a structured auxiliary witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection ideality controls attainable original vectors but not multiplicity, boundedness, integrality, or structure of auxiliary witnesses.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is projection-ideal for \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{No full lifted-fiber exactness follows from projection ideality alone.}
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Ideality Does Not Control Auxiliary Fibers

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization characterization restricted to original-coordinate objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\), then for every \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\inf_{(x,y)\in R}c^{\mathsf T}x=\inf_{x\in S}c^{\mathsf T}x,\qquad \sup_{(x,y)\in R}c^{\mathsf T}x=\sup_{x\in S}c^{\mathsf T}x.\] Conversely, if \(R\) is nonempty and convex, \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R)\) is closed, and the supremum equalities hold for every \(c\), then \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection ideality preserves every original-variable linear objective, and equality of all support values characterizes it when the projected relaxation is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a nonempty convex lifted relaxation.
For the converse, \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R)\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_x(R)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\iff \sigma_{\operatorname{proj}_x(R)}(c)=\sigma_S(c)\ \forall c.
knowledge_statements.title: Original-Linear-Objective Characterization

children.title: Ideality in Extended Space
children.top_down_role: Ideality assessed using the full lifted formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Ideality in Extended Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness of the entire lifted feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) be the intended lifted feasible set and let \(R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) be a convex relaxation of \(Z\). The formulation \(R\) is ideal in extended space when \[R=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(Z).\] This equality concerns the full lifted coordinates rather than only their original-variable projection. If \(\operatorname{conv}(Z)\) is closed, the closure may be omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted formulation is ideal in extended space when its entire relaxation equals the closed convex hull of the intended lifted feasible points.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) is the intended lifted feasible set.
\(R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) is a convex relaxation containing \(Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(Z)\).

source_refs.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-function test for equality of the full lifted sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\supseteq Z\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Then \[R=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(Z)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sup_{w\in R}c^{\mathsf T}w=\sup_{w\in Z}c^{\mathsf T}w\quad\text{for every }c\in\mathbb R^{n+p},\] with values interpreted in the extended reals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex lifted relaxation is ideal exactly when every lifted-space linear objective has the same supremum over it and the intended lifted set.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(Z)\iff \sigma_R(c)=\sigma_Z(c)\ \forall c.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Objective Characterization of Extended-Space Ideality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection Ideality Does Not Imply Extended-Space Ideality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation caused by surplus auxiliary fibers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{0,1\}\), \(Z=\{(0,0),(1,0)\}\), and \(R=[0,1]\times[0,1]\). Then \[\operatorname{proj}_x(R)=[0,1]=\operatorname{conv}(S),\qquad R\ne\operatorname{conv}(Z)=[0,1]\times\{0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact original-variable projection can coexist with surplus auxiliary points, so projection ideality does not imply full lifted-space ideality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_x(R)=\operatorname{conv}(S)\text{ but }R\ne\operatorname{conv}(Z).
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Ideality Does Not Imply Extended-Space Ideality

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Extreme-Point Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded polyhedral relaxations with designated integer coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be a nonempty polytope and let \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\) index the coordinates required to be integral. The condition \[\operatorname{ext}(P)\subseteq\{z\in\mathbb{R}^d:z_I\in\mathbb{Z}^{|I|}\}\] certifies \[P=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(P\cap\{z\in\mathbb{R}^d:z_I\in\mathbb{Z}^{|I|}\}\bigr).\] Nonextreme points of \(P\) may still be fractional in the designated coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every vertex of a nonempty polytope is integral in the designated coordinates, the polytope equals the convex hull of its integer-feasible points, although nonvertices may be fractional.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is a nonempty polytope.
\(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\) indexes coordinates required to be integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ext}(P)\subseteq\{z\in\mathbb{R}^d:z_I\in\mathbb{Z}^{|I|}\}\) certifies \(P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\{z\in\mathbb{R}^d:z_I\in\mathbb{Z}^{|I|}\})\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertex Test Fails Without Recession Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the polytope certificate for unbounded polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[P=\{t(1,\sqrt2):t\ge0\}\subseteq\mathbb R^2\] and designate both coordinates as integral. Its only vertex is \((0,0)\), but \(P\cap\mathbb Z^2=\{(0,0)\}\). Therefore \[P\ne\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb Z^2).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An irrational unbounded ray has an integral vertex but no other integer points, so vertex integrality alone is insufficient without recession control.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{ext}(P)\subseteq\mathbb Z^2\text{ but }P\ne\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb Z^2).
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Test Fails Without Recession Control

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary-and-sufficient form of the seed certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polytope \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) and designated coordinates \(I\), \[P=\operatorname{conv}\{z\in P:z_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\ \text{for every }v\in\operatorname{ext}(P).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polytope equals the convex hull of its mixed-integer points exactly when every vertex is integral in the designated coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty polytope.
\(I\) designates the integer coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\{z:z_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\})\iff \operatorname{ext}(P)\subseteq\{z:z_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Integrality Equivalence for Polytopes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral characterization and closure properties of total unimodularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Corrects the extract's dimensionally inconsistent right-hand-side domain and records the three stated results.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\). Then \(A\) is totally unimodular if and only if, for every \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}\), every vertex of \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}\) is integral. If \(A\) is totally unimodular, then for every \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}\), every vertex of \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) is integral. Moreover, \(A\) is totally unimodular if and only if \(A^{\top}\) is totally unimodular, if and only if \([A\ I_m]\) is totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an integral matrix, total unimodularity is equivalent to integral vertices for every associated nonnegative inequality polyhedron with an integral right-hand side. It implies the analogous equality-form result and is equivalent to total unimodularity of the transpose and of the matrix obtained by adjoining an identity matrix.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}
b\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ TUM}\iff\forall b\in\mathbb{Z}^{m},\ \operatorname{vert}\{x:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{n};\quad A\text{ TUM}\Rightarrow\forall b\in\mathbb{Z}^{m},\ \operatorname{vert}\{x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{n};\quad A\text{ TUM}\iff A^{\top}\text{ TUM}\iff[A\ I_m]\text{ TUM}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Row-partition sufficient condition for total unimodularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the sufficient row-partition criterion and its immediate signed-column special case; illustrative figure material is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\{-1,0,1\}^{m\times n}\). Suppose each column contains at most two nonzero entries and the rows can be partitioned as \(R_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}R_2=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) so that, for every column \(j\) with two nonzero entries, \(\sum_{i\in R_1}a_{ij}=\sum_{i\in R_2}a_{ij}\). Then \(A\) is totally unimodular. In particular, any \(\{-1,0,1\}\)-matrix containing at most one \(+1\) and at most one \(-1\) in each column is totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A {-1,0,1} matrix is totally unimodular if every column has at most two nonzeros and the rows can be split into two sets whose column sums agree for each column with two nonzeros. Consequently, at most one +1 and at most one -1 per column is sufficient.
assumptions_latex: A\in\{-1,0,1\}^{m\times n}
|\{i:a_{ij}\ne0\}|\le2\quad\forall j
R_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}R_2=\{1,\ldots,m\}
\sum_{i\in R_1}a_{ij}=\sum_{i\in R_2}a_{ij}\quad\text{for every column }j\text{ with two nonzero entries}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is totally unimodular}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent-Space Dual Certificate for Unique Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard sufficient certificate for nuclear-norm recovery of a fixed low-rank matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_0=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\), let \[T=\{UY^{\mathsf T}+ZV^{\mathsf T}:Y,Z\text{ arbitrary}\},\] and suppose \(\ker(\mathcal A)\cap T=\{0\}\). If some \(y\) satisfies \[P_T(\mathcal A^*y)=UV^{\mathsf T},\qquad \|P_{T^\perp}(\mathcal A^*y)\|_2<1,\] then \(X_0\) is the unique minimizer of \(\min\{\|X\|_*:\mathcal A(X)=\mathcal A(X_0)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Injectivity on the tangent space plus a strict nuclear-norm dual certificate guarantees unique recovery of the target matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is linear.
\(X_0=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\) is feasible.
\(\ker(\mathcal A)\cap T=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X_0\text{ is the unique nuclear-norm minimizer}.

notation.meaning: tangent space at the fixed-rank target

knowledge_statements.title: Tangent-Space Dual Certificate for Unique Recovery

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact uniqueness condition for a fixed feasible target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\) be linear and satisfy \(\mathcal A(X_0)=b\). Then \(X_0\) is the unique minimizer of \[\min_X\{\|X\|_*:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\] if and only if \[\|X_0+H\|_*>\|X_0\|_*\quad\text{for every }0\ne H\in\ker\mathcal A.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible matrix is uniquely recovered by nuclear-norm minimization exactly when every nonzero feasible null-space perturbation strictly increases its nuclear norm.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is linear.
\(\mathcal A(X_0)=b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X_0\text{ is the unique minimizer}\iff \|X_0+H\|_*>\|X_0\|_*\ \forall H\in\ker\mathcal A\setminus\{0\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Nuclear-Norm Null-Space Recovery Criterion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Low Rank and Feasibility Do Not Ensure Unique Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure under a nonidentifying measurement map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A(X)=\operatorname{tr}(X)\) on \(\mathbb S^2\), let \(b=1\), and let \(X_0=\operatorname{Diag}(1,0)\). Both \(X_0\) and \(X_1=\operatorname{Diag}(0,1)\) are feasible and have nuclear norm one; indeed every positive-semidefinite trace-one matrix is optimal. Thus the feasible rank-one target \(X_0\) is not uniquely recovered.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Trace-only measurements leave many matrices tied with a feasible rank-one target under nuclear-norm minimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X_0\text{ is rank one and feasible but is not uniquely recovered}.
knowledge_statements.title: Low Rank and Feasibility Do Not Ensure Unique Recovery

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{A}:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R}^q\) is linear.
\(X_0\) has rank at most \(r\) and satisfies \(\mathcal{A}(X_0)=b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_0\) is the unique minimizer of \(\min\{\|X\|_*:\mathcal{A}(X)=b\}\).

notation.meaning: the tangent space of the rank-rank manifold at the target

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nuclear-norm recovery of a fixed low-rank matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_0=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\), let \(T=\{UY^{\mathsf T}+ZV^{\mathsf T}:Y,Z\text{ arbitrary}\}\), and assume \(\ker(\mathcal A)\cap T=\{0\}\). If there exists \(y\in\mathbb{R}^q\) such that \[P_T(\mathcal A^*y)=UV^{\mathsf T},\qquad \|P_{T^\perp}(\mathcal A^*y)\|_2<1,\] then \(X_0\) is the unique minimizer of \(\min\{\|X\|_*:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\), certifying exact low-rank recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Injectivity on the tangent space plus a strict nuclear-norm dual certificate guarantees unique recovery of the target low-rank matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Low-Rank Recovery Exactness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tangent-space injectivity and strict dual-certificate conditions form a plausible sufficient certificate and the content kind fits, but the exact uniqueness theorem has no source or locator and should not be relied upon without one.

children.title: Divergent Exactness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where integrality evidence and rank evidence yield different conclusions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Logical Independence of Integral-Vertex and Low-Rank-Recovery Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aligned matrix examples separating the two sibling certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Designate the diagonal entries as integer coordinates. First, let \[Q_1=\{\operatorname{Diag}(t,1-t):0\le t\le1\}.\] Its two extreme points have integral designated coordinates, but nuclear-norm minimization over \(Q_1\) does not uniquely recover \(\operatorname{Diag}(1,0)\), since every \(X\in Q_1\) has \(\|X\|_*=1\). Conversely, let \[Q_2=\{\operatorname{Diag}(1/2,0)\}.\] Nuclear-norm minimization over \(Q_2\) uniquely recovers its rank-one member, while its sole extreme point is nonintegral in the first designated coordinate. Hence neither certificate implies the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A diagonal line segment has integral vertices but no unique nuclear-norm recovery, while a nonintegral rank-one singleton is uniquely recovered but fails vertex integrality.
assumptions_latex: Integrality is assessed on the designated diagonal coordinates.
Low-rank recovery means uniqueness of the stated nuclear-norm minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Integral extreme-point exactness and unique low-rank recovery are logically independent.}

notation.meaning: matrix feasible regions used in the two separation examples

knowledge_statements.title: Logical Independence of Integral-Vertex and Low-Rank-Recovery Exactness

assumptions_latex: Integrality and rank are assessed on specified coordinate or matrix representations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither integral extreme-point exactness nor rank-one extreme-point exactness implies the other.

notation.meaning: the set of positive semidefinite trace-one matrices

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete separation of integrality and low-rank extreme-point criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polytope \(P=[0,1]^2\) has only integral extreme points, but under the matrix embedding \((x_1,x_2)\mapsto\operatorname{Diag}(x_1,x_2)\), its extreme point \((1,1)\) has rank \(2\). Conversely, for \(d\geq2\), the spectrahedron \[\mathcal D_d=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^d:\operatorname{tr}(X)=1\}\] has precisely the rank-one projectors as extreme points, while their entries vary continuously and are generally nonintegral. Hence the two exactness regimes are logically independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit box has integral vertices but a rank-two diagonal vertex, while density matrices have rank-one extreme points with generally nonintegral entries.
knowledge_statements.title: Divergent Exactness Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The examples separate integral vertices from rank-one extreme points, but the sibling low-rank record concerns nuclear-norm recovery rather than rank-one extreme-point exactness. The second example also requires an explicit choice of designated integral coordinates. A source and a precise common comparison framework are needed.

children.title: Domain-Restricted Envelopes
children.top_down_role: Envelope families over bounded intervals, boxes, polyhedra, and other structured domains.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain convention resolving the ambiguity in restricted convexity and concavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For this envelope family, \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is assumed nonempty and convex. Convexity and concavity on \(D\) use the usual Jensen inequalities for all \(x,y\in D\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricted envelopes are taken over a nonempty convex domain, with convexity and concavity understood intrinsically on that domain.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta x+(1-\theta)y\in D\) for \(x,y\in D\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\), so the standard convexity and concavity inequalities are well defined.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Domain Convention

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of functions unchanged by restricted enveloping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) on a nonempty convex domain, \[\operatorname{vex}_D f=f\iff f\text{ is convex on }D,\qquad \operatorname{cav}_D f=f\iff f\text{ is concave on }D.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function equals its restricted convex envelope exactly when it is convex, and equals its restricted concave envelope exactly when it is concave.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a nonempty convex domain.
\(f:D\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{vex}_D f=f\iff f\) is convex, and \(\operatorname{cav}_D f=f\iff f\) is concave.
knowledge_statements.title: Envelope Exactness Criterion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of restricting the domain while retaining the same function values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(D_1\subseteq D_2\) are nonempty convex sets and \(f:D_2\to\mathbb R\), then on \(D_1\), \[\operatorname{vex}_{D_1}(f|_{D_1})\ge \operatorname{vex}_{D_2}f,\qquad \operatorname{cav}_{D_1}(f|_{D_1})\le \operatorname{cav}_{D_2}f.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shrinking the domain can only raise the convex envelope and lower the concave envelope.
assumptions_latex: \(D_1\subseteq D_2\) are nonempty convex domains.
\(f:D_2\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{vex}_{D_1}(f|_{D_1})\ge\operatorname{vex}_{D_2}f\) and \(\operatorname{cav}_{D_1}(f|_{D_1})\le\operatorname{cav}_{D_2}f\) on \(D_1\).
knowledge_statements.title: Domain Monotonicity of Envelopes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise representation of restricted envelopes on a finite-dimensional convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex and \(f:D\to\mathbb R\). For \(x\in D\), \[\operatorname{vex}_D f(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\lambda_i f(x_i):\lambda\in\Delta_{n+1},\ x_i\in D,\ \sum_i\lambda_i x_i=x\right\},\] and \[\operatorname{cav}_D f(x)=\sup\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\lambda_i f(x_i):\lambda\in\Delta_{n+1},\ x_i\in D,\ \sum_i\lambda_i x_i=x\right\}.\] The values may be \(-\infty\) or \(+\infty\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricted envelopes are obtained by minimizing or maximizing averaged function values over convex decompositions using at most n+1 points.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and convex.
\(f:D\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The restricted envelope values admit the displayed convex-combination formulas with at most \(n+1\) support points.

notation.meaning: simplex of nonnegative weights summing to one

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Convex-Combination Formula

assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty.
\(f:D\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{vex}_D f\leq f\leq\operatorname{cav}_D f\) on \(D\).

notation.meaning: the convex envelope of f on D
the concave envelope of f on D

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex and concave envelopes relative to a specified domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The domain-restricted convex envelope is \[\operatorname{vex}_D f(x)=\sup\{g(x):g\text{ is convex on }D,\ g\leq f\text{ on }D\},\] and the domain-restricted concave envelope is \[\operatorname{cav}_D f(x)=\inf\{h(x):h\text{ is concave on }D,\ h\geq f\text{ on }D\}.\] These envelopes depend on \(D\); changing an interval, box, polyhedron, or other admissible domain can change both functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The restricted convex envelope is the greatest convex underestimator on the chosen domain, and the concave envelope is the least concave overestimator there.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Restricted Envelopes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The envelope formulas are standard on convex domains, but the assumption permits an arbitrary nonempty domain without defining convexity and concavity on a nonconvex set. An authoritative source must establish the intended domain convention and hypotheses.

children.title: Epigraph-Hypograph Hull Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Envelope geometry expressed through convexified epigraphs and hypographs.

children.title: Convexified Epigraph Geometry
children.top_down_role: Hull geometry supporting convex underestimation through epigraph representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph example exhibiting a missing limiting boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) satisfy \(f(x)=0\) for \(x>0\) and \(f(x)=+\infty\) for \(x\le0\). Then \[\operatorname{epi}f=(0,\infty)\times[0,\infty)\] is convex but not closed, whereas \[\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)=[0,\infty)\times[0,\infty)=\operatorname{epi}(f^{**}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An already convex epigraph may omit boundary points, so closed convexification cannot generally be replaced by convexification alone.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=0\) for \(x>0\) and \(f(x)=+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\ne\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Cannot Generally Be Dropped

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of the possibly nonclosed convex envelope from vertical fibers of the unclosed epigraph hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), let \(E=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}_D f)\). For \(x\in\operatorname{conv}D\), \[g(x):=\inf\{t:(x,t)\in E\}=\inf\left\{\sum_i\lambda_i f(x_i):\sum_i\lambda_i x_i=x,\ \lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1,\ x_i\in D\right\}.\] The set \(E\) is upward closed, but its lower boundary need not be attained; \(\operatorname{cl}E\) is the epigraph of the lower-semicontinuous convex closure of \(g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertical fibers of the convexified epigraph yield the convex-envelope value, while closure supplies missing limiting boundaries.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty.
\(f:D\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x)=\inf\{t:(x,t)\in\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}_D f)\}\), and closing the hull gives the lower-semicontinuous convex closure.

notation.meaning: unclosed convex hull of the restricted epigraph

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Hull Fiber Formula

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper.
\(f\) admits an affine minorant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}(f^{**})=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convexification of an epigraph in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}:t\geq f(x)\}\), the closed convexified epigraph satisfies \[\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)=\operatorname{epi}(f^{**}).\] Equivalently, \(f^{**}\) is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function majorized by \(f\). If \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\) is already closed, the closure on the left is unnecessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed convex hull of a proper function's epigraph is the epigraph of its Fenchel biconjugate, the closed convex envelope.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexified Epigraph Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional epigraph–biconjugate identity is appropriately scoped by properness and an affine minorant and fits the representation leaf, but no inspectable Fenchel–Moreau source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Convexified Hypograph Geometry
children.top_down_role: Hull geometry supporting concave overestimation through hypograph representations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Cannot Generally Be Dropped from a Hypograph Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign-reflected example showing the need for closure or upper-semicontinuous regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) satisfy \(f(x)=0\) for \(x>0\) and \(f(x)=-\infty\) for \(x\le0\). Then \[\operatorname{hypo}f=(0,\infty)\times(-\infty,0]\] is convex but not closed, and its closure adds \(\{0\}\times(-\infty,0]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex hypograph can omit a limiting boundary, so closed convexification and upper-semicontinuous regularization are genuinely needed.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=0\) for \(x>0\) and \(f(x)=-\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{hypo}f)\ne\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{hypo}f)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Cannot Generally Be Dropped from a Hypograph Hull

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise recovery of a concave envelope from the upper boundary of a convexified hypograph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), let \(H=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{hypo}_D f)\). For \(x\in\operatorname{conv}D\), \[h(x):=\sup\{t:(x,t)\in H\}=\sup\left\{\sum_i\lambda_i f(x_i):\sum_i\lambda_i x_i=x,\ \lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1,\ x_i\in D\right\}.\] The set \(H\) is downward closed, but its upper boundary need not be attained; \(\operatorname{cl}H\) is the hypograph of the upper-semicontinuous concave closure of \(h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Upper fibers of the convexified hypograph give the concave-envelope value, while closure supplies missing limiting boundaries.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty.
\(f:D\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h(x)=\sup\{t:(x,t)\in\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{hypo}_D f)\}\), and closing the hull gives the upper-semicontinuous concave closure.

notation.meaning: unclosed convex hull of the restricted hypograph

knowledge_statements.title: Hypograph-Hull Fiber Formula

assumptions_latex: \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
\(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is upper semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{hypo}(\operatorname{cav}_D f)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{hypo}_D f)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed-hull form of concave-envelope geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(H_f=\{(x,t)\in D\times\mathbb{R}:t\le f(x)\}\). The upper-semicontinuous concave envelope \(\operatorname{cav}_D f\), namely the least upper-semicontinuous concave majorant of \(f\) on \(D\), satisfies \[\operatorname{hypo}(\operatorname{cav}_D f)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}H_f.\] Consequently, its value at \(x\in D\) is \[\operatorname{cav}_D f(x)=\sup\{t:(x,t)\in\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}H_f\}.\] Thus convexifying and closing the hypograph produces exactly the geometry of the closed concave envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed convex hull of a function's hypograph is the hypograph of its upper-semicontinuous concave envelope.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexified Hypograph Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closed-hypograph representation is mathematically plausible and fits the leaf, but the selected upper-semicontinuous envelope version and its hypotheses have no cited source.

children.title: Epigraph–Hypograph Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between the two envelope representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise correspondence between convex underestimation and concave overestimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty convex domain \(D\) and real-valued function \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), \[\operatorname{vex}_D f=-\operatorname{cav}_D(-f),\qquad \operatorname{cav}_D f=-\operatorname{vex}_D(-f),\] with equality in the extended-real sense. The same sign identities exchange the lower-semicontinuous convex and upper-semicontinuous concave envelope versions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negation exchanges restricted convex and concave envelopes, including their closed semicontinuous versions.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and convex.
\(f:D\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{vex}_D f=-\operatorname{cav}_D(-f)\) and \(\operatorname{cav}_D f=-\operatorname{vex}_D(-f)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Envelope Sign Duality
Epigraph–Hypograph Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign-reflection correspondence, including convexification and closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the linear involution \(T:\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\to\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\) by \(T(x,t)=(x,-t)\). For every nonempty \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and extended-real function \(f:D\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), one has \[T(\operatorname{epi}_D f)=\operatorname{hypo}_D(-f),\qquad T(\operatorname{hypo}_D f)=\operatorname{epi}_D(-f).\] Because \(T\) is an invertible continuous linear map, every \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\) satisfies \[T(\operatorname{conv}S)=\operatorname{conv}T(S),\qquad T(\operatorname{cl}S)=\operatorname{cl}T(S).\] Hence closed convex epigraph-hull statements correspond to closed convex hypograph-hull statements under vertical sign reflection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ambient vertical sign reflection maps epigraphs to hypographs and commutes with convex hulls and closure.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty.
\(f:D\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is an extended-real function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(\operatorname{epi}_D f)=\operatorname{hypo}_D(-f)\) and \(T(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}S)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}T(S)\).

children.title: Closed-Hull Requirements
children.top_down_role: Topological conditions affecting closed envelope representations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compactness Sufficient Condition for Closed Hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sufficient condition under which closure is redundant in a hull formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is compact, then \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is compact and therefore closed. Hence \[\operatorname{conv}S=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}S,\] so closing the hull introduces no additional points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, a compact generating set has a compact, hence closed, convex hull.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is compact.
\(d<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}S\text{ is compact and }\operatorname{conv}S=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}S.
knowledge_statements.title: Compactness Sufficient Condition for Closed Hulls

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\) is an epigraph or hypograph set.
The intended envelope is closed and convex or closed and concave, respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unclosed hull is exact precisely when \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is closed; otherwise the exact closed envelope requires \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact condition for omitting closure from an envelope hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\) be the relevant epigraph or hypograph. The closed convexified set is \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}S\). Therefore the formula using the unclosed hull, \(\operatorname{conv}S\), represents the closed envelope exactly if and only if \[\operatorname{conv}S=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}S,\] equivalently, if and only if \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is closed. Without this condition, replacing the closed hull by the ordinary convex hull can omit boundary points and can yield an envelope that is not lower semicontinuous in the epigraph case or not upper semicontinuous in the hypograph case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closure may be omitted from a hull formula exactly when the ordinary convex hull is already closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Hull Requirements

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closedness equivalence is correct and the condition kind fits the leaf, but no source supports the envelope interpretation or semicontinuity consequences.

children.title: Recession-Cone Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility of envelope constructions with unbounded-domain directions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Incompatible Recession Can Produce a Nonclosed Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure example showing that closed disjuncts alone do not ensure closed convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y\ge 1/x\}\) and \(C_2=\{(0,0)\}\). Both sets are closed and convex, with \(\operatorname{rec}C_1=\mathbb R_+^2\) and \(\operatorname{rec}C_2=\{0\}\). For every \(a>0\), points of \(\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)\) converge to \((a,0)\), but \((a,0)\notin\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed convex sets with incompatible recession cones can have a nonclosed convex hull of their union.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)\ne\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Incompatible Recession Can Produce a Nonclosed Hull

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition for a finite family of nonempty closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite family \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is recession-cone compatible when there is a closed convex cone \(K\) such that \(\operatorname{rec}C_i=K\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite family is recession-cone compatible when all members have the same recession cone.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) are nonempty closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}C_1=\cdots=\operatorname{rec}C_m=K\).
knowledge_statements.title: Common Recession-Cone Compatibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common Recession Is Sufficient, Not Necessary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness boundary for the common-recession sufficient condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Equality of recession cones is not necessary for closedness. For \(C_1=\{(t,0):t\ge0\}\) and \(C_2=\{(0,t):t\ge0\}\), one has \(\operatorname{rec}C_1=C_1\ne C_2=\operatorname{rec}C_2\), while \(\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)=\mathbb R_+^2\), which is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different recession cones do not by themselves force nonclosedness; the common-cone hypothesis is sufficient rather than necessary.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are the two nonnegative coordinate rays in \(\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}C_1\ne\operatorname{rec}C_2\) and \(\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)=\mathbb R_+^2\).
knowledge_statements.title: Common Recession Is Sufficient, Not Necessary

assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) are nonempty closed convex sets.
Their recession cones coincide: \(\operatorname{rec}C_i=K\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i)\) is closed and has recession cone \(K\).

notation.meaning: recession cone of a closed convex set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-family sufficient condition for closed convexification of unbounded sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) are nonempty closed convex sets and \[\operatorname{rec}C_1=\cdots=\operatorname{rec}C_m=K.\] Then their disjunctive convexification is closed: \[\operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i\right).\] Moreover, \[\operatorname{rec}\operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=K.\] Thus a common asymptotic geometry prevents convex combinations from converging to finite boundary points that are absent from the unclosed hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite family of closed convex sets with a common recession cone has a closed convex hull of its union.
knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Cone Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a substantive closed-convexification theorem whose exact hypotheses and recession-cone conclusion require an authoritative theorem locator.

children.title: Nonclosed Envelope Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Validity failures associated with unattained limits or missing boundary points.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}S=\{(0,0)\}\cup\mathbb{R}_{++}^2\) is not closed, while \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}S=\mathbb{R}_+^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete nonclosed convex hull caused by incompatible recession behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb{R}^2:u>0,\ v\ge 1/u\},\qquad S=C\cup\{(0,0)\}.\] The set \(C\) is closed and convex, but \[\operatorname{conv}S=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(x,y):x>0,\ y>0\}.\] Hence \(\operatorname{conv}S\) omits every nonzero point on the coordinate axes and is not closed, whereas \[\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}S=\mathbb{R}_+^2.\] Consequently, an envelope obtained from the ordinary hull can omit limiting boundary values that appear in the closed envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex branch joined to the origin can have a nonclosed convex hull whose closure adds entire boundary rays.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Envelope Pathologies

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample and hull calculations are internally correct and fit the pathology leaf, but the record supplies neither a source nor an explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Inclusion-Projection Dominance Order
children.top_down_role: Geometric dominance in a common space or after elimination of auxiliary variables.

children.title: Common-Space Set Inclusion
children.top_down_role: Geometric strength comparisons between relaxations expressed in the same variables.

assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq R_1\subseteq R_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
The problem is minimization and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in R_1}c^\top x\ge\inf_{x\in R_2}c^\top x\), so \(R_1\) is at least as strong as \(R_2\).

notation.meaning: two relaxations in the same variable space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization convention for relaxations in one variable space.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq R_1\subseteq R_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), where \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) are relaxations of the same minimization problem. For every \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), set \(b_i(c)=\inf\{c^\top x:x\in R_i\}\). Set inclusion gives \[b_1(c)\ge b_2(c).\] Thus \(R_1\) is the stronger common-space relaxation. If the infimum over \(F\) is finite, its lower bounds satisfy \[b_2(c)\le b_1(c)\le\inf_{x\in F}c^\top x.\] For maximization, the inequality directions reverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among minimization relaxations in the same space, the smaller feasible set gives at least as large a lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Common-Space Set Inclusion

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between common-space containment and uniform linear-objective dominance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_1,R_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty closed convex sets. Then \[R_1\subseteq R_2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \inf_{x\in R_1}c^\top x\ge \inf_{x\in R_2}c^\top x\quad\text{for every }c\in\mathbb{R}^n,\] where the infima may be extended-real. Equivalently, inclusion is characterized by the corresponding ordering of all support functions under the supremum convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonempty closed convex sets in one space, inclusion is equivalent to dominance for every linear objective.
assumptions_latex: \(R_1,R_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) are nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_1\subseteq R_2\iff \inf_{R_1}c^\top x\ge\inf_{R_2}c^\top x\) for every \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\).

notation.meaning: sets compared in the same variable space

knowledge_statements.title: Universal Linear-Bound Characterization of Inclusion

children.title: Projected-Space Dominance
children.top_down_role: Strength comparisons after auxiliary variables have been eliminated.

knowledge_statements.title: Projected-Space Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominance after eliminating formulation-specific auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(Z_1\) and \(Z_2\) be auxiliary-variable spaces, and let \(Q_i\subseteq X\times Z_i\) satisfy \(F\subseteq P_i:=\pi_X(Q_i)\) for \(i\in\{1,2\}\), where \(F\subseteq X\). Formulation \(1\) dominates formulation \(2\) in projected-space strength when \[P_1\subseteq P_2.\] For every \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), this inclusion implies \[\inf_{(x,z_1)\in Q_1}c^\top x\ge\inf_{(x,z_2)\in Q_2}c^\top x.\] This comparison concerns objectives depending only on the original variables and does not require \(Z_1\) and \(Z_2\) to coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lifted formulations are compared by inclusion of their original-variable projections, even when their auxiliary spaces differ.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(F\subseteq X\).
\(Q_i\subseteq X\times Z_i\) are lifted relaxations with \(F\subseteq P_i:=\pi_X(Q_i)\) for \(i\in\{1,2\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Formulation \(1\) dominates formulation \(2\) in original-space strength exactly when \(P_1\subseteq P_2\).
