knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective Dominance Determines Only Closed Convexified Projections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on recovering raw projected containment from linear-objective comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For arbitrary nonempty projected sets \(P_1,P_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\inf_{x\in P_1}c^\top x\ge\inf_{x\in P_2}c^\top x\quad\text{for every }c\in\mathbb{R}^n\] holds if and only if \[\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(P_1)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(P_2).\] Consequently, universal original-variable linear-bound dominance implies raw containment \(P_1\subseteq P_2\) only under additional conditions, such as both projections being closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All linear objectives identify containment of the closed convexified projections, not necessarily containment of the raw projections.
assumptions_latex: \(P_1,P_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform linear-bound dominance is equivalent to \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(P_1)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(P_2)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Objective Dominance Determines Only Closed Convexified Projections

children.title: Dominance Reversal Under Lifting
children.top_down_role: Cases where ordering changes across original and extended spaces.

assumptions_latex: Both sets are projected onto their first coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi_X(Q_1)\subsetneq\pi_X(Q_2)\), although neither \(Q_1\subseteq Q_2\) nor \(Q_2\subseteq Q_1\).

notation.meaning: two sets represented in a common lifted display space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Apparent reversal or loss of dominance caused by comparing auxiliary coordinates.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[Q_1=[0,1]\times[0,2],\qquad Q_2=[0,2]\times\{0\},\] and let \(\pi_X(x,z)=x\). Then \[\pi_X(Q_1)=[0,1]\subsetneq[0,2]=\pi_X(Q_2),\] so the first formulation is stronger after projection, but \(Q_1\nsubseteq Q_2\) and \(Q_2\nsubseteq Q_1\). Thus auxiliary-space inclusion may disappear or appear to conflict with projected dominance. A genuine reversal is impossible under a common projection and valid inclusion, because \(Q_2\subseteq Q_1\) would imply \(\pi_X(Q_2)\subseteq\pi_X(Q_1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected dominance need not produce inclusion between lifted sets; a true reversal under the same projection is impossible.
knowledge_statements.title: Dominance Reversal Under Lifting

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Non-invariance of lifted-set inclusion under equivalent choices of auxiliary coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq X\times Z\) represent \(P=\pi_X(Q)\), and let \(T:Z\to Z\) be invertible. The reparameterized lift \[Q_T=\{(x,Tz):(x,z)\in Q\}\] has the same projection, \(\pi_X(Q_T)=P\). Nevertheless, for a fixed comparison lift \(\widehat Q\subseteq X\times Z\), an inclusion involving \(Q\) and \(\widehat Q\) need not persist after replacing \(Q\) by \(Q_T\). Thus lifted-set inclusion is meaningful only after declaring a common auxiliary embedding and coordinate identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent auxiliary reparameterizations preserve original-space projections but can change inclusion relations between lifted sets.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq X\times Z\) is a lifted set.
\(T:Z\to Z\) is invertible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi_X(Q_T)=\pi_X(Q)\), while inclusion comparisons with another fixed lift need not be preserved.
knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Coordinate Dependence of Lifted Inclusion

children.title: Bound-Gap Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Strength comparison through relaxation bounds and optimization gaps.

children.title: Objective-Bound Strength
children.top_down_role: Comparison of relaxation quality through resulting objective bounds.

assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq R_1,R_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) are relaxations of one minimization instance.
\(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and all relevant infima are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Relaxation \(R_1\) is at least as strong for objective \(c\) when \(b_{R_1}(c)\ge b_{R_2}(c)\).

notation.meaning: relaxation lower bound for objective c

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-specific lower-bound ordering for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization relaxation \(R\supseteq F\), define \[b_R(c)=\inf_{x\in R}c^\top x,\qquad z_F(c)=\inf_{x\in F}c^\top x.\] Then \(b_R(c)\le z_F(c)\). For two relaxations, \(R_1\) is at least as strong as \(R_2\) for the specified objective \(c\) precisely when \[b_{R_1}(c)\ge b_{R_2}(c).\] The certificate is objective-specific: it compares valid lower bounds even when neither relaxation contains the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed minimization objective, the relaxation producing the larger valid lower bound is stronger.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Bound Strength

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximization counterpart of the accepted minimization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a maximization problem with \(F\subseteq R\), define \[u_R(c)=\sup_{x\in R}c^\top x,\qquad z_F(c)=\sup_{x\in F}c^\top x.\] Then \(u_R(c)\ge z_F(c)\). For two relaxations, \(R_1\) is at least as strong as \(R_2\) for the specified objective \(c\) precisely when \[u_{R_1}(c)\le u_{R_2}(c),\] because the smaller valid upper bound is tighter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed maximization objective, the relaxation producing the smaller valid upper bound is stronger.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq R_1,R_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) are relaxations of one maximization instance.
The relevant suprema are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_1\) is at least as strong as \(R_2\) for \(c\) when \(u_{R_1}(c)\le u_{R_2}(c)\).

notation.meaning: relaxation upper bound for a maximization objective

knowledge_statements.title: Maximization Objective-Bound Strength

children.title: Integrality-Gap Quality
children.top_down_role: Comparison through residual separation from discrete optimal values.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality-Gap Quality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization gaps with explicit sign restrictions for ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem with finite optimum \(z^*\) and finite relaxation bound \(b_R\le z^*\), the additive integrality gap is \[g_R=z^*-b_R\ge0.\] A smaller \(g_R\) is better, and \(g_R=0\) certifies equality of the relaxation and original optimal values. If additionally \(z^*>0\) and \(b_R>0\), the multiplicative gap may be defined as \[\rho_R=\frac{z^*}{b_R}\ge1,\] with values nearer \(1\) being better. Ratio gaps are not invariant under objective translation and are unsuitable when the denominator is nonpositive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gap quality measures the difference between the true optimum and a relaxation bound; a ratio gap requires a strictly positive relaxation bound.
assumptions_latex: \(z^*\) is the finite optimum of a minimization problem.
\(b_R\le z^*\) is the finite optimum of relaxation \(R\).
The multiplicative convention is used only when \(z^*>0\) and \(b_R>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The additive gap is \(z^*-b_R\); when \(z^*>0\) and \(b_R>0\), the ratio gap is \(z^*/b_R\), with smaller values indicating better quality.

notation.meaning: multiplicative integrality gap under positive-value assumptions

source_refs.locator: 3.4.2 The geometry of a max-cut relaxation p. 58

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4.2 The geometry of a max-cut relaxation p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Incumbent Upper Certificate for the Integrality Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computable upper bound on the true additive integrality gap when the original optimum is unknown.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem, let \(b_R\le z^*\) be a finite valid relaxation lower bound and let an original-feasible incumbent have finite value \(u\). Then \[0\le z^*-b_R\le u-b_R.\] Hence the computable incumbent-to-relaxation difference upper-bounds the unknown additive integrality gap. If \(u=b_R\), then \(u=z^*=b_R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible incumbent value minus a relaxation lower bound upper-bounds the unknown additive integrality gap, and equality at zero certifies the common optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(b_R\le z^*\) is a finite valid lower bound for a minimization problem.
An original-feasible incumbent has finite value \(u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le z^*-b_R\le u-b_R\), and \(u=b_R\) implies \(u=z^*=b_R\).
knowledge_statements.title: Incumbent Upper Certificate for the Integrality Gap

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of what a zero integrality gap certifies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A zero additive integrality gap, \(z^*=b_R\), certifies equality of optimal values only. It does not imply \(R=\operatorname{conv}(F)\), nor that every relaxation optimizer is original-feasible. For example, with \(F=\{0\}\), \(R=[0,1]\), and the constant-zero objective, both optimal values are zero, but \(R\ne\operatorname{conv}(F)\) and every point of \(R\), including nonoriginal points, is a relaxation optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero integrality gap certifies value equality, not hull equality or recoverability of every relaxed optimizer.
assumptions_latex: A relaxation and its original minimization problem have the same finite optimal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^*=b_R\) need not imply \(R=\operatorname{conv}(F)\) or that every optimizer of the relaxation belongs to \(F\).
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Gap Value-Exactness Boundary

children.title: Instance-Dependent Quality Ordering
children.top_down_role: Variation in bound or gap rankings across objectives and model instances.

assumptions_latex: Relaxation quality is measured by minimization lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ordering reverses between objectives \(c=(1,-1)\) and \(c'=(-1,1)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective dependence of quality when relaxations are incomparable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{(0,0)\}\), \(R_1=[0,1]\times\{0\}\), and \(R_2=\{0\}\times[0,1]\). Both sets relax \(F\), but neither contains the other. For \(c=(1,-1)\), \[b_1(c)=0>-1=b_2(c),\] so \(R_1\) gives the stronger minimization bound. For \(c'=(-1,1)\), \[b_1(c')=-1<0=b_2(c'),\] so \(R_2\) is stronger. Therefore objective-bound or integrality-gap quality defines an instance-and-objective-dependent ordering unless set inclusion supplies uniform dominance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incomparable relaxations can exchange which one is stronger when the objective changes.
knowledge_statements.title: Instance-Dependent Quality Ordering

children.title: Strength–Size–Tractability Tradeoffs

assumptions_latex: \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) are exact or relaxed convex formulations of the same original-variable problem.
Size and tractability are measured in specified representation and oracle models.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Set strength, representation size, and tractability form a multi-criterion ordering; improving one coordinate does not alone order the others.

cost of optimization or separation in a fixed computational model

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Associate with each formulation \(R\) the triple \((P(R),s(R),\tau(R))\), where \(P(R)\) is its projected relaxation, \(s(R)\) its encoding size, and \(\tau(R)\) its optimization or separation cost in fixed models. For minimization, \(P(R_1)\subseteq P(R_2)\) certifies greater strength, but it implies neither \(s(R_1)\le s(R_2)\) nor \(\tau(R_1)\le\tau(R_2)\). Lifting may increase \(s(R)\) while improving separability or conic representability. Accordingly, formulations are Pareto-compared across strength, size, and tractability unless an application supplies an explicit scalar cost model.

Therefore projected-set strength alone cannot establish a representation-size or runtime ordering.

children.title: Bilinear Box Envelopes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Corner-Vertex Representation of the Bilinear Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent vertex description of the graph hull of one bounded continuous bilinear term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S=\{(x,y,w):x\in[L_x,U_x],\ y\in[L_y,U_y],\ w=xy\}\), let \(V=\{(a,b,ab):a\in\{L_x,U_x\},\ b\in\{L_y,U_y\}\}\). Then \(\operatorname{conv}(S)=\operatorname{conv}(V)\). If \(L_x<U_x\) and \(L_y<U_y\), these four points are affinely independent, so the hull is a tetrahedron whose facets are the four McCormick inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bilinear graph hull is the tetrahedron generated by the four lifted corners of the factor box.
assumptions_latex: \(L_x<U_x\) and \(L_y<U_y\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}(S)=\operatorname{conv}\{(a,b,ab):a\in\{L_x,U_x\},\ b\in\{L_y,U_y\}\}.

notation.meaning: Four lifted corners of the factor box.

knowledge_statements.title: Corner-Vertex Representation of the Bilinear Hull
Bilinear Box Envelopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact McCormick convex hull for one bounded continuous bilinear term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L_x<U_x\), \(L_y<U_y\), and \(S=\{(x,y,w):L_x\le x\le U_x,\ L_y\le y\le U_y,\ w=xy\}\). Then \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is exactly the polytope defined by the box bounds and
\[
\begin{aligned}
w&\ge L_xy+L_yx-L_xL_y,\\
w&\ge U_xy+U_yx-U_xU_y,\\
w&\le U_xy+L_yx-U_xL_y,\\
w&\le L_xy+U_yx-L_xU_y.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first two affine functions form the convex envelope of \(xy\) on the box, while the last two form its concave envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graph of a bounded bilinear product has an exact four-inequality polyhedral convex hull, known as the McCormick envelope.
assumptions_latex: \(L_x<U_x\) and \(L_y<U_y\).
\((x,y)\in[L_x,U_x]\times[L_y,U_y]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) equals the four-inequality McCormick polytope.

notation.meaning: Lifted variable representing the product xy.
Graph of the bilinear term over the box.

children.title: Binary–Continuous Product Hulls

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Disjunctive Extended Form of the Binary Product Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-combination formulation separating inactive and active values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L<U\). The convex hull of \(\{(b,x,w):b\in\{0,1\},\ L\le x\le U,\ w=bx\}\) has the extended formulation \[0\le b\le1,\quad x=x^0+x^1,\quad L(1-b)\le x^0\le U(1-b),\quad Lb\le x^1\le Ub,\quad w=x^1.\] Eliminating \(x^0,x^1\) gives the four standard binary–continuous product inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Splitting the continuous value into inactive and active contributions gives an ideal extended formulation equivalent to the compact hull.
assumptions_latex: \(L<U\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_{b,x,w}Q=\operatorname{conv}\{(b,x,bx):b\in\{0,1\},\ x\in[L,U]\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Extended Form of the Binary Product Hull
Binary–Continuous Product Hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear hull of a binary activation multiplied by a bounded scalar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L<U\) and \(S=\{(b,x,w):b\in\{0,1\},\ L\le x\le U,\ w=bx\}\). Its convex hull is the set of \((b,x,w)\) satisfying \(0\le b\le1\), \(L\le x\le U\), and
\[
Lb\le w\le Ub,\qquad x-U(1-b)\le w\le x-L(1-b).
\]
For \(b=0\), these inequalities force \(w=0\); for \(b=1\), they force \(w=x\). Thus the formulation is ideal: every extreme point of its continuous relaxation has an integral activation coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four linear inequalities give the exact convex hull of a bounded continuous variable multiplied by a binary activation.
assumptions_latex: \(L\le x\le U\) with finite \(L<U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(b,x,w):0\le b\le1,\ L\le x\le U,\ Lb\le w\le Ub,\ x-U(1-b)\le w\le x-L(1-b)\}\).

children.title: Multilinear Convexification
children.top_down_role: Recursive and direct convexification families for products with more than two factors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a tree-structured relaxation for a bounded multilinear monomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a full binary tree with leaves \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). Process internal nodes upward. At a node with child quantities \(p\in[L_p,U_p]\) and \(q\in[L_q,U_q]\), introduce \(r\), impose the four bilinear box-envelope inequalities for \(r=pq\), and assign \([L_r,U_r]\) as the exact interval product of the child intervals before processing its parent. The root represents \(w\). The resulting lifted polyhedron contains every point satisfying \(w=\prod_i x_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursive bilinearization chooses a factorization tree, propagates interval bounds upward, and applies one McCormick envelope at each internal node.
assumptions_latex: All leaf intervals are finite.
Every internal-node interval is valid for its child product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{(x,w):w=\prod_i x_i,\ x_i\in[L_i,U_i]\}\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_{x,w}R_T.

notation.meaning: Recursive relaxation associated with tree T.

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Bilinearization Procedure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-size contrast for one n-factor multilinear product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The direct vertex-mixture hull uses \(2^n\) nonnegative weights, one normalization equation, \(n\) equations recovering \(x\), and one equation recovering \(w\). A full binary factorization tree has \(n-1\) internal nodes, so recursive bilinearization uses \(n-1\) auxiliary product variables and \(4(n-1)\) envelope inequalities, in addition to valid propagated bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The direct exact vertex hull has exponentially many weights, whereas a recursive bilinear tree has linear size but may be weaker.
assumptions_latex: All original and intermediate factors have finite valid interval bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{direct weights}=2^n,\quad \text{recursive products}=n-1,\quad \text{recursive envelope inequalities}=4(n-1).
knowledge_statements.title: Direct and Recursive Formulation Sizes
Multilinear Convexification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact vertex formulation and recursive bilinear relaxation for bounded multilinear products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n[L_i,U_i]\), let \(V\) be its \(2^n\) vertices, and let \(m(x)=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\). The convex hull of the graph of \(m\) is represented exactly by
\[
\lambda_v\ge0,\quad \sum_{v\in V}\lambda_v=1,\quad x=\sum_{v\in V}\lambda_vv,\quad w=\sum_{v\in V}\lambda_vm(v).
\]
Alternatively, a binary factorization tree may introduce intermediate products and apply a bilinear box envelope at each internal node. Its projection is a valid convex relaxation, but for \(n\ge3\) it can be weaker than the direct vertex hull and can depend on the chosen factorization tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multilinear graph has an exact vertex-mixture hull; recursively applying bilinear envelopes is smaller but may be weaker and grouping-dependent.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge2\) and every bound \(L_i<U_i\) is finite.
\(m(x)=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\) on the box \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The vertex formulation equals \(\operatorname{conv}\{(x,m(x)):x\in B\}\); recursive bilinear lifting is an outer relaxation.

notation.meaning: Vertex set of the factor box.
Convex-combination weight assigned to vertex v.

children.title: Fixed-Curvature Atoms

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent-Cut Approximation for a Convex Atom
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite outer approximations using supporting tangents and the endpoint secant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:[L,U]\to\mathbb R\) be finite and convex, and let \(T\subseteq[L,U]\) be finite. For each \(t\in T\), choose \(g_t\in\partial f(t)\) and set \(\ell_t(x)=f(t)+g_t(x-t)\). Then \[\max_{t\in T}\ell_t(x)\le f(x)\le s_f(x).\] Thus \(\{(x,w):L\le x\le U,\ \max_{t\in T}\ell_t(x)\le w\le s_f(x)\}\) is a polyhedral outer approximation of the exact graph hull. Enlarging \(T\) can only strengthen it. For concave \(f\), apply the construction to \(-f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Supporting tangents give nested polyhedral approximations of the atom side of a fixed-curvature graph hull; the endpoint secant is exact on the opposite side.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is finite and convex on \([L,U]\).
A subgradient exists at every selected tangent point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{graph}f)\subseteq\{(x,w):\max_{t\in T}\ell_t(x)\le w\le s_f(x)\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Tangent-Cut Approximation for a Convex Atom

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence guarantee for nested tangent-cut approximations on the interval interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_k\subset(L,U)\) be nested finite sets whose union is dense in \((L,U)\), and choose \(g_t\in\partial f(t)\) for each selected point. With \(q_k(x)=\max_{t\in T_k}[f(t)+g_t(x-t)]\), one has \(q_k\le q_{k+1}\le f\) and \(q_k(x)\uparrow f(x)\) for every \(x\in(L,U)\). The convergence is uniform on every compact subinterval of \((L,U)\). Each added tangent contributes one affine inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested tangents placed densely converge monotonically to a finite convex atom on the interval interior, uniformly away from the endpoints.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is finite and convex on \([L,U]\).
\(T_k\subset T_{k+1}\subset(L,U)\) and \(\bigcup_kT_k\) is dense in \((L,U)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q_k\uparrow f\text{ pointwise on }(L,U)\text{ and uniformly on each }[L+\varepsilon,U-\varepsilon].

notation.meaning: Maximum of supporting tangents selected through iteration k.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense Tangent Refinement Convergence
Fixed-Curvature Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact univariate envelopes when curvature has one sign throughout a compact interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:[L,U]\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. If \(f\) is convex, its convex envelope is \(f\) itself and its concave envelope is the endpoint secant
\[
s_f(x)=\frac{U-x}{U-L}f(L)+\frac{x-L}{U-L}f(U).
\]
Hence the convex hull of the graph is \(\{(x,w):L\le x\le U,\ f(x)\le w\le s_f(x)\}\). If \(f\) is concave, the roles reverse: the convex envelope is \(s_f\), the concave envelope is \(f\), and the same graph-hull description holds with \(s_f(x)\le w\le f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed-curvature univariate atom, the atom and its endpoint secant are the two exact graph envelopes.
assumptions_latex: \(L<U\) are finite.
\(f\) is continuous and either convex or concave on \([L,U]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The graph hull lies exactly between \(f\) and its endpoint secant \(s_f\), ordered according to curvature.

notation.meaning: Affine secant through the endpoint values of f.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The atom/secant graph-hull representation is mathematically standard and correctly restricted to continuous fixed-curvature functions on a compact interval, but no source locator is provided.

children.title: Changing-Curvature Atoms

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate for affine pieces of differentiable univariate envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be continuous on \(I=[L,U]\) and differentiable near asserted interior contacts. Let \(L\le a<b\le U\), and let \(\ell\) be the chord through \((a,f(a))\) and \((b,f(b))\). If \(\ell(x)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in I\), then \(\ell=\operatorname{vex}_I f\) on \([a,b]\). If \(\ell(x)\ge f(x)\) for every \(x\in I\), then \(\ell=\operatorname{cav}_I f\) on \([a,b]\). At an interior contact endpoint, differentiability implies \(f'(a)=f'(b)=(f(b)-f(a))/(b-a)\) for each endpoint lying in \((L,U)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contact chord that lies globally on the correct side of the atom is an exact envelope segment; interior contacts satisfy tangent–chord slope equations.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuous on \([L,U]\).
\(L\le a<b\le U\).
\(f\) is differentiable near each asserted interior contact endpoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ell\le f\text{ on }I\Rightarrow \ell=\operatorname{vex}_I f\text{ on }[a,b],\quad \ell\ge f\text{ on }I\Rightarrow \ell=\operatorname{cav}_I f\text{ on }[a,b].

notation.meaning: Chord through the two contact points.

review_flags: revised_builder_claim:global dominance is required on the entire active interval, not merely between the contact points
knowledge_statements.title: Contact-Chord Envelope Certificate
Changing-Curvature Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact one-dimensional envelopes across intervals containing curvature transitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I=[L,U]\) be a nonempty compact interval and let \(f:I\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. Its convex and concave envelopes are
\[
\operatorname{vex}_I f(x)=\min_{\substack{s,t\in I,\ 0\le\lambda\le1\\x=\lambda s+(1-\lambda)t}}\bigl[\lambda f(s)+(1-\lambda)f(t)\bigr]
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{cav}_I f(x)=\max_{\substack{s,t\in I,\ 0\le\lambda\le1\\x=\lambda s+(1-\lambda)t}}\bigl[\lambda f(s)+(1-\lambda)f(t)\bigr].
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{conv}\{(x,f(x)):x\in I\}=\{(x,w):x\in I,\ \operatorname{vex}_I f(x)\le w\le\operatorname{cav}_I f(x)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous univariate function on a compact interval, the exact convex and concave envelopes are obtained by optimizing over two-point chords with the requested argument as barycenter; the graph hull is the region between them.
assumptions_latex: \(I=[L,U]\) is a nonempty compact interval.
\(f:I\to\mathbb R\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}\{(x,f(x)):x\in I\}=\{(x,w):x\in I,\ \operatorname{vex}_I f(x)\le w\le\operatorname{cav}_I f(x)\}\).

notation.meaning: Greatest convex minorant of f on I.
Least concave majorant of f on I.

children.title: Singular-Domain Atom Failure Boundary

children.title: Singular Atom Envelopes
children.top_down_role: Envelope behavior near poles, roots, or other singular locations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Two-Sided Finite Envelopes Across a Pole
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Envelope failure caused by a reciprocal singularity inside the active interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L<0<U\), \(D=[L,0)\cup(0,U]\), and \(f(x)=1/x\). No finite-valued concave function on \([L,U]\) can overestimate \(f\) on \(D\), since \(f(x)\to+\infty\) as \(x\downarrow0\). No finite-valued convex function on \([L,U]\) can underestimate \(f\) on \(D\), since \(f(x)\to-\infty\) as \(x\uparrow0\). Thus no finite convex-under/concave-over envelope pair exists across the pole.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Opposite divergence on the two sides of the reciprocal pole prevents a finite two-sided envelope pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No finite-valued convex underestimator and concave overestimator bound \(f\) on \(D\).

notation.meaning: The interval excluding the reciprocal singularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Two-Sided Finite Envelopes Across a Pole
Singular Atom Envelopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite envelopes for a singular atom on a compact interval separated from its singularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the reciprocal atom \(f(x)=1/x\) on an interval \([L,U]\) with \(0<L<U\), \(f\) is convex and its exact graph hull is
\[
\left\{(x,w):L\le x\le U,\ \frac1x\le w\le \frac{U-x}{U-L}\frac1L+\frac{x-L}{U-L}\frac1U\right\}.
\]
On an interval \(L<U<0\), \(f\) is concave, so the two bounds reverse. These finite envelope representations require the interval to lie inside one connected component of the natural domain and to remain a positive distance from the singularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reciprocal envelopes are finite and exact on a compact interval confined to one side of zero; curvature determines their ordering.
assumptions_latex: Either \(0<L<U\) or \(L<U<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The graph hull is bounded by \(1/x\) and its endpoint secant, ordered according to the sign component.

notation.meaning: Active interval separated from the reciprocal singularity.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reciprocal graph-hull formulas and curvature ordering are correct for compact intervals strictly on one side of zero and fit the singular-envelope container, but no supporting citation is supplied.

children.title: Natural-Domain Restrictions
children.top_down_role: Convexification limited by the intrinsic domain of a nonlinear atom.

knowledge_statements.title: Natural-Domain Restrictions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain condition required before constructing finite continuous atom envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be an atom and let \(I=[L,U]\) be its proposed argument interval. A finite continuous-envelope construction is admissible only if
\[
I\subseteq D,\qquad I\text{ lies in one connected component of }D,\qquad \sup_{x\in I}|f(x)|<\infty.
\]
A sufficient check is that \(I\) is compact and contained in the interior of one domain component on which \(f\) is continuous. If any condition fails, the interval must be tightened, split along excluded points, or represented using a formulation explicitly encoding separate domain components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An atom interval must stay within one continuous natural-domain component and have finite range before finite envelope construction is valid.
assumptions_latex: \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) is a real-valued atom.
\(I=[L,U]\) is the active argument interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite continuous envelopes require \(I\subseteq D\), component consistency, and bounded values of \(f\) on \(I\).

notation.meaning: Natural real-valued domain of the atom.
Active interval for the atom argument.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated domain, component, and boundedness conditions appropriately describe finite continuous interval-envelope admissibility, but the necessity and sufficient-check claims need an authoritative source locator.

children.title: Discontinuity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Representation issues arising at jumps or excluded limiting points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexification Can Fill an Excluded Domain Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of disconnected-domain semantics under ordinary graph convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=[-1,0)\cup(0,1]\) and \(f(x)=0\) on \(D\). Although the graph excludes \(x=0\), \[(0,0)=\tfrac12(-a,0)+\tfrac12(a,0)\qquad(0<a\le1),\] so \((0,0)\in\operatorname{conv}\{(x,f(x)):x\in D\}\). Hence the graph hull projects onto \([-1,1]\), not the disconnected domain \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexifying a graph over a disconnected domain can fill excluded argument values even when the function is bounded and continuous on each component.
assumptions_latex: \(f\equiv0\) on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in\operatorname{proj}_x\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{graph}_D f)\setminus D.

notation.meaning: Disconnected domain with an excluded interior point.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexification Can Fill an Excluded Domain Point
Discontinuity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of finite envelope models when an interval crosses an unbounded discontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f(x)=1/x\) on \(D=[-1,0)\cup(0,1]\). There is no finite convex function \(g:[-1,1]\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(g(x)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in D\): as \(x\uparrow0\), the right-hand side tends to \(-\infty\), whereas finite convex \(g\) is continuous at zero. Likewise, no finite concave \(h:[-1,1]\to\mathbb R\) can satisfy \(h(x)\ge f(x)\) on \(D\), because \(f(x)\to+\infty\) as \(x\downarrow0\). Thus no finite two-sided graph envelope exists across the discontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Crossing zero destroys finite reciprocal envelopes: one side is unbounded below and the other unbounded above.
assumptions_latex: Candidate envelopes are finite-valued on \([-1,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No finite convex underestimator and finite concave overestimator can jointly cover the reciprocal graph across zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Expression-Graph Lifting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Auxiliary-variable lifting of a factorable expression along its directed acyclic graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a factorable expression be represented by a directed acyclic graph with input nodes \(z_i=x_i\) and operation nodes \(z_v=\phi_v((z_u)_{u\in\operatorname{pa}(v)})\). Its lifted graph formulation consists of all node variables together with these defining equalities and the original constraints written using the root variables. Replacing every equality by an outer graph relaxation \(R_v\) gives
\[
(z_v,(z_u)_{u\in\operatorname{pa}(v)})\in R_v
\]
for each operation node. The projection of the resulting lifted set onto the original variables contains the original feasible set; exact node graph formulations yield an exact projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Introduce one variable per expression node, then relax each local operation graph; projecting the lifted system gives a valid global relaxation.
assumptions_latex: The expression graph is finite and acyclic.
Each operation node has a valid outer graph relaxation \(R_v\) over its propagated bounds.

children.title: Monotone Composition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Composition structure classified by increasing or decreasing outer behavior.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise propagation of inner bounds through a multivariate monotone outer function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\ell_i(x)\le g_i(x)\le u_i(x)\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), with all resulting vectors in a box \(B\). Let \(h:B\to\mathbb R\) be nondecreasing in coordinates \(I_+\) and nonincreasing in coordinates \(I_-\), where \(I_+\cup I_-=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Define \(a_i=\ell_i\) and \(b_i=u_i\) for \(i\in I_+\), and \(a_i=u_i\) and \(b_i=\ell_i\) for \(i\in I_-\). Then \(h(a(x))\le h(g(x))\le h(b(x))\) for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose each endpoint according to the outer function's monotonicity in that coordinate to obtain valid composite lower and upper bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_i(x)\le g_i(x)\le u_i(x)\) for every coordinate and every \(x\).
\(h\) has the stated coordinatewise monotonicity throughout a box containing the propagated vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h(a(x))\le h(g(x))\le h(b(x))\) for every \(x\).

notation.meaning: Increasing and decreasing coordinate sets of the outer function.
Endpoint vectors producing the composite lower and upper bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Monotone Bound Propagation
Monotone Composition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound propagation of inner-function bounds through a monotone outer function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\ell(x)\le g(x)\le u(x)\) for every \(x\in X\), and suppose all three values lie in an interval \(J\). If \(h:J\to\mathbb R\) is nondecreasing, then
\[
h(\ell(x))\le h(g(x))\le h(u(x))\qquad(x\in X).
\]
If \(h\) is nonincreasing, then
\[
h(u(x))\le h(g(x))\le h(\ell(x))\qquad(x\in X).
\]
Thus composition preserves the orientation of lower and upper bounds for an increasing outer map and reverses it for a decreasing outer map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An increasing outer function preserves inner bound order; a decreasing outer function reverses it.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell(x)\le g(x)\le u(x)\) for all \(x\in X\).
The outer function \(h\) is monotone on an interval containing all propagated values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Monotonicity determines whether composition preserves or reverses the inner bounds.

notation.meaning: Lower and upper bounds for the inner function.
Interval on which the outer function is monotone.

children.title: Curvature Composition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Composition structure classified by convex or concave curvature.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multivariate curvature composition using coordinatewise outer monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be convex, let \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):X\to\mathbb R^m\), and let \(h:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) be convex. If, for every coordinate \(i\), either \(h\) is nondecreasing in coordinate \(i\) and \(g_i\) is convex, \(h\) is nonincreasing in coordinate \(i\) and \(g_i\) is concave, or \(g_i\) is affine, then \(h\circ g\) is convex on \(X\). Dually, if \(h\) is concave, increasing coordinates receive concave inner functions, decreasing coordinates receive convex inner functions, and all remaining inner functions are affine, then \(h\circ g\) is concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multivariate outer function preserves convexity or concavity when each inner coordinate has the curvature selected by the outer function's monotonicity in that coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is convex.
The stated coordinatewise monotonicity holds throughout \(\mathbb R^m\), or throughout an order-convex region containing every value used in the comparison.
Each \(g_i\) has the stated curvature on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\circ g\) has the asserted curvature on \(X\).

notation.meaning: Coordinate functions of the inner mapping.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Curvature Composition Rule
Curvature Composition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard sufficient rules for convexity or concavity of scalar compositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:X\to J\) and \(h:J\to\mathbb R\), where \(X\) is convex and \(J\) is an interval. The composition \(h\circ g\) is convex if either: \(h\) is convex and nondecreasing while \(g\) is convex; \(h\) is convex and nonincreasing while \(g\) is concave; or \(g\) is affine and \(h\) is convex. It is concave under the dual rules: concave nondecreasing \(h\) with concave \(g\), concave nonincreasing \(h\) with convex \(g\), or affine \(g\) with concave \(h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer curvature, outer monotonicity, and inner curvature jointly determine standard sufficient composition-curvature rules.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is convex and \(g(X)\subseteq J\).
\(J\) is an interval on which the stated curvature and monotonicity properties hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under any listed regime, \(h\circ g\) has the asserted convexity or concavity on \(X\).

notation.meaning: Interval containing the range of the inner function.

children.title: Mixed Composition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where available monotonicity or curvature information is insufficient for a direct relaxation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Curvature Alone Does Not Determine Composite Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of convex-with-convex composition without compatible outer monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(X=[-1,1]\), let \(g(x)=x^2\) and \(h(t)=(t-\tfrac12)^2\) for \(t\in[0,1]\). Both \(g\) and \(h\) are convex, but \((h\circ g)(x)=x^4-x^2+\tfrac14\) is not convex on \(X\). The outer function decreases on \([0,\tfrac12]\) and increases on \([\tfrac12,1]\), while \(g(X)=[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex inner and outer functions can have a nonconvex composition when the outer function changes monotonicity over the attained inner range.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) and \(h\) are convex, but \(h\circ g\) is not convex on \(X\).

notation.meaning: Range attained by the inner function.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature Alone Does Not Determine Composite Curvature
Mixed Composition Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of bound composition when the outer map changes monotonicity on the propagated range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Outer monotonicity cannot be omitted from bound propagation. On \(X=[-1,1]\), let \(g(x)=x\), \(\ell(x)=-1\), and \(h(t)=t^2\). Although \(\ell(x)\le g(x)\) for every \(x\in X\), the putative composed lower bound fails:
\[
h(\ell(x))=1\not\le x^2=h(g(x))
\]
for every \(x\in(-1,1)\). The failure occurs because \(h\) changes monotonicity at zero and the propagated range crosses that point. Sound propagation therefore requires splitting the range into monotone regimes or constructing an envelope of the full composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the outer function changes monotonicity over the inner range, composing an inner bound can reverse validity; range splitting or direct envelopes are required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The implication \(\ell\le g\Rightarrow h\circ\ell\le h\circ g\) fails when \(h\) is not nondecreasing on the propagated range.

notation.meaning: A valid lower bound for the inner function.
Outer function with a monotonicity transition at zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exactness and Dominance of Sign-Aware Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness and monotone tightening for fixed local affine propagation rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a directed acyclic expression graph and fixed local affine coefficient vectors. If every selected child estimator is exact on \(X\), then the propagated parent estimator is exact whenever the corresponding local affine relation is exact. More generally, replacing a selected child lower estimator by a pointwise larger valid lower estimator, or a selected child upper estimator by a pointwise smaller valid upper estimator, cannot weaken the resulting parent estimator when the local coefficients and sign-based selections remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact child bounds and an exact local affine relation propagate exactness; tightening a selected child bound can only tighten the parent bound.

\text{Local affine coefficients and their signs are fixed}

knowledge_statements.title: Exactness and Dominance of Sign-Aware Propagation
Affine Relaxation Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological propagation of affine underestimators and overestimators through a factorable expression graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a directed acyclic expression graph have input domain \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\). For every child \(i\) of node \(v\), suppose \(L_i(x)\le z_i(x)\le U_i(x)\) on \(X\), with \(L_i,U_i\) affine. Given valid local inequalities \(\phi_v(s)\ge a_0+\sum_i a_i s_i\) and \(\phi_v(s)\le b_0+\sum_i b_i s_i\) on the child range, set
\[L_v=a_0+\sum_{a_i\ge0}a_iL_i+\sum_{a_i<0}a_iU_i,\qquad U_v=b_0+\sum_{b_i\ge0}b_iU_i+\sum_{b_i<0}b_iL_i.\]
Initialize input nodes exactly, process nodes topologically, and output the root pair \((L_r,U_r)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Substitute child lower or upper affine bounds according to coefficient signs in each valid local affine relaxation, proceeding from inputs to the root.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) is the domain on which all propagated bounds are required to hold.
Each local affine inequality is valid over the complete range of its child variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_v(x)\le z_v(x)\le U_v(x)\) for every processed node \(v\) and every \(x\in X\).

children.title: Subgradient Separation Propagation
children.top_down_role: Transfer of local supporting information from component convexifications.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local chain step for a convex nondecreasing scalar outer function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:X\to\mathbb R\) be convex and let \(\phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be convex and nondecreasing. Set \(F=\phi\circ h\). At \(\bar x\in X\), choose \[p\in\partial h(\bar x),\qquad \alpha\in\partial\phi(h(\bar x)).\] Then \(\alpha\ge0\) and \[q=\alpha p\in\partial F(\bar x).\] Thus the child subgradient may be propagated through the node by multiplication with a nonnegative outer subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex nondecreasing scalar composition, multiplying a child subgradient by an outer subgradient gives a valid subgradient of the composition.
assumptions_latex: h:X\to\mathbb R\text{ is convex}
\phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\text{ is convex and nondecreasing}
\partial h(\bar x)\ne\varnothing\text{ and }\partial\phi(h(\bar x))\ne\varnothing
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha p\in\partial(\phi\circ h)(\bar x)
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone-Composition Subgradient Propagation
Subgradient Separation Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting-hyperplane separation from a convex root underestimator assembled through the expression graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:X\to\mathbb R\) be a convex underestimator of an expression-graph root \(f\), and let \((\bar x,\bar t)\) satisfy \(F(\bar x)>\bar t\). Select \(q\in\partial F(\bar x)\), propagating subgradients from active local estimators by the convex subdifferential chain and sum rules whenever their qualification and monotonicity conditions hold. Then
\[t\ge F(\bar x)+q^{\mathsf T}(x-\bar x)\]
is valid for every \((x,t)\) with \(x\in X\) and \(t\ge f(x)\), while it is violated by \((\bar x,\bar t)\). Thus \((F(\bar x),q)\) is a directly checkable separation certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgradient of a convex root underestimator produces a supporting inequality that is valid for the original epigraph and separates any point lying below it.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is convex and \(F\) is finite and convex at \(\bar x\).
\(F(x)\le f(x)\) for all \(x\in X\).
Any graphwise subgradient chain rule used satisfies its regularity and monotonicity hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\ge F(\bar x)+q^{\mathsf T}(x-\bar x)\) is valid and excludes \((\bar x,\bar t)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Invalid Child Ranges Can Invalidate a Propagated Chord
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by applying a local affine estimator beyond its certified range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(s)=s^2\), the chord through \((-1,1)\) and \((1,1)\) is \(U(s)=1\), and \[h(s)\le U(s)\qquad(s\in[-1,1]).\] If this upper estimator is propagated for a child whose actual range contains \(2\), then \[h(2)=4>1=U(2).\] Hence an estimator certified only on an incorrectly narrow child range can make the propagated relaxation invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The constant chord one upper-bounds a square on minus one to one but fails at two, showing that an incorrect child range can invalidate propagation.
assumptions_latex: U\text{ is certified only on }[-1,1]
2\text{ belongs to the actual child range}
knowledge_statements.title: Invalid Child Ranges Can Invalidate a Propagated Chord

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is the declared domain of the expression graph.
Every local estimator used in propagation is valid on the complete joint range of its child variables.
Repeated occurrences that denote the same original variable remain consistently coupled.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_v(x)\le z_v(x)\le U_v(x)\) is preserved at every processed node under the stated validity, coupling, and sign or monotonicity conditions; without such conditions, global validity is not guaranteed.

notation.meaning: an intermediate node value and its lower estimator

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:composition of bounds requires sign or monotonicity control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient safeguards for preserving validity during local-estimator propagation, and circumstances in which validity is no longer guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an expression graph be evaluated on a declared domain \(X\). Local-estimator propagation preserves validity when every local estimator is valid on the complete joint range of its child variables, repeated occurrences of each original variable remain consistently coupled, and every bound substitution respects coefficient signs or the applicable composition monotonicity. If one of these safeguards is absent, global validity is not guaranteed. For example, if \(u(x)\ge L(x)\) on \(X\), one cannot in general infer \(u(x)^2\ge L(x)^2\) when the possible values cross zero, because \(s\mapsto s^2\) is not monotone on such a range. Enlarging a valid child range can weaken a propagated relaxation, whereas using an invalid range or composition rule can make it invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validity is preserved under range-valid local estimators, consistent repeated variables, and sign-correct or monotonic composition. Without these safeguards, a propagated inequality need not remain valid.

children.title: Bound-Dependent Weakness
children.top_down_role: Strength loss caused by missing, broad, or poorly scaled variable domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Dependent Weakness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative deterioration of factorable relaxations as variable bounds widen or disappear.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,y\in[-M,M]\), the McCormick relaxation of \(z=xy\) permits, at \(x=y=0\), every \(z\in[-M^2,M^2]\), whereas the exact graph requires \(z=0\). Hence the relaxation gap at that point grows as \(M^2\). More generally, local convexification formulas for products and other factorable atoms depend on finite operand bounds; broad bounds enlarge their feasible envelopes, poor scaling magnifies numerical and geometric weakness, and absent finite bounds can make the usual envelope inequalities unavailable. Bound tightening can therefore strictly strengthen the propagated relaxation without changing the original feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bilinear term, widening symmetric operand bounds to size M creates a root relaxation gap of order M squared; missing finite bounds may prevent envelope construction.
assumptions_latex: The bilinear graph is relaxed by the four McCormick inequalities over \([-M,M]^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \((x,y)=(0,0)\), the relaxed width in \(z\) is \(2M^2\), while the exact width is zero.

notation.meaning: lifted variable representing the product xy

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:direct specialization of the McCormick bilinear envelope

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed McCormick specialization is correct: at x=y=0 it permits z in [-M^2,M^2], giving width 2M^2. The failure-boundary content kind matches the bound-dependent weakness leaf. No source with a section, theorem, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Factorization Dependence
children.top_down_role: Strength differences among algebraically equivalent expression graphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Factorization Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraically identical expressions can yield different relaxations when represented by different expression graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(x\in[-1,1]\), represent \(w=x^2\) either as a square atom or as the product of two occurrences of \(x\). The square-atom convex relaxation includes \(w\ge x^2\) and \(w\le1\), so at \(x=0\) it requires \(0\le w\le1\). Applying only the bilinear McCormick inequalities to \(w=x\cdot x\) gives \(w\ge2x-1\), \(w\ge-2x-1\), and \(w\le1\), which permit \(-1\le w\le1\) at \(x=0\). Thus algebraic equivalence does not imply equal expression-graph relaxation strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treating a square as a dedicated atom is stronger than applying a generic bilinear envelope to two identical operands, despite algebraic equivalence.
assumptions_latex: No additional square-specific or semidefinite strengthening is added to the product formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The product-graph relaxation strictly contains the square-atom relaxation at \(x=0\).

notation.meaning: lifted value of the expression x squared

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:the displayed envelopes directly establish factorization-dependent strength

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is correct under the stated absence of square-specific strengthening: the generic bilinear relaxation permits negative w at x=0 while the square-atom relaxation does not. The counterexample kind fits this leaf, but the record lacks inspectable supporting evidence.

children.title: Repeated-Variable Coupling
children.top_down_role: Coupling structure among multiple occurrences of a common variable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal and redundant equality systems enforcing consistency among copies of one variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(O_j\) contain \(m\ge1\) copies and let \(G=(O_j,E)\) be undirected. The equalities \(x_j^{(o)}=x_j^{(o')}\) for \(\{o,o'\}\in E\) enforce equality of all copies if and only if \(G\) is connected. For an oriented vertex-edge incidence matrix \(B_G\), this is equivalently \(\ker(B_G^{\mathsf T})=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}\). A connected equality graph has rank \(m-1\), and a spanning tree supplies \(m-1\) independent equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All copies are equal exactly when their equality graph is connected; a spanning tree gives a minimal independent coupling system.
assumptions_latex: Every vertex represents an occurrence of the same scalar variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:B_G^{\mathsf T}x=0\}=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}\iff G\text{ is connected}.
knowledge_statements.title: Connected Equality-Graph Representation
Repeated-Variable Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact consistency constraints for multiple expression-graph occurrences of one original variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose an original variable \(x_j\in D_j\subseteq\mathbb R\) appears at occurrence set \(O_j\). An occurrence lifting introduces a copy \(x_j^{(o)}\in D_j\) for each \(o\in O_j\). The repeated-variable coupling set is
\[C_j=\left\{(x_j^{(o)})_{o\in O_j}:x_j^{(o)}=x_j^{(o')}\text{ for all }o,o'\in O_j\right\}.\]
Equivalently, one may retain a master variable \(x_j\) and impose \(x_j^{(o)}=x_j\) for every occurrence. These equalities are part of the exact lifted representation, not optional relaxation cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Copies introduced for different occurrences of the same original variable must all equal one another, or a common master variable, in an exact lifting.
assumptions_latex: Each occurrence in \(O_j\) denotes the same original scalar variable \(x_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact occurrence lifting requires \((x_j^{(o)})_{o\in O_j}\in C_j\).

notation.meaning: set of occurrences of original variable j
equality-coupling set for all copies of variable j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict relaxation loss caused by treating dependent occurrences as independent bounded variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in[0,1]\) and consider the identically zero expression \(y=x-x\). If its two occurrences are replaced by independent copies \(x^{(1)},x^{(2)}\in[0,1]\) without the coupling equality \(x^{(1)}=x^{(2)}\), the lifted equation \(y=x^{(1)}-x^{(2)}\) permits every \(y\in[-1,1]\). The exact expression permits only \(y=0\). Thus interval-valid local propagation can be strictly weaker than the original dependency structure when repeated occurrences are independently relaxed.

knowledge_statements.title: Occurrence-Aware Strengthening
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strengthening an occurrence-relaxed formulation by restoring shared-variable consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be any lifted relaxation formed with occurrence copies \(x_j^{(o)}\), and let \(C=\bigcap_j C_j\) impose equality among copies of each original variable. Then \(R\cap C\subseteq R\), so adding occurrence coupling never weakens the relaxation. If the only discrepancy between the lifted expression graph and the original graph is duplication of variables, projection after imposing \(C\) restores the original shared-variable semantics. Partial equalities, aggregate consistency equations, or valid cuts implied by \(C\) give intermediate strengthenings while preserving every exactly lifted feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equality constraints or valid consequences linking repeated occurrences shrink the relaxation and can restore the semantics of the original shared variables.
assumptions_latex: All occurrence copies associated with index \(j\) represent the same original variable.
\(R\) is valid for the uncoupled lifted formulation.

children.title: Two-Term Disjunction Geometry
children.top_down_role: Convexification structure for unions containing two alternatives.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded two-term hull representation under a shared recession cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty closed convex sets with \(\operatorname{rec}(C_1)=\operatorname{rec}(C_2)=K\). Define \(0C_i:=K\) and \(\lambda C_i:=\{\lambda c:c\in C_i\}\) for \(\lambda>0\). Then \[\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)=\left\{x=x^1+x^2:x^i\in\lambda_iC_i,\ \lambda_i\ge0,\ \lambda_1+\lambda_2=1\right\},\] and this convex hull is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For closed convex alternatives sharing one recession cone, the perspective formulation remains exact at zero weights and the two-term hull is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1,C_2\) are nonempty closed convex sets.
\(\operatorname{rec}(C_1)=\operatorname{rec}(C_2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed formulation is exact and \(\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Common-Recession Closedness Regime
Two-Term Disjunction Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex-hull lifting for a union of two bounded convex alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C_1,C_2\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty compact convex sets. With \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2\ge0\), define \(\lambda_iC_i=\{\lambda_i c:c\in C_i\}\). Then
\[\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)=\left\{x:x=x^1+x^2,\ x^i\in\lambda_iC_i,\ \lambda_1+\lambda_2=1,\ \lambda_i\ge0\right\}.\]
The multipliers select a term at the disjunctive extremes \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\), while fractional multipliers describe convex combinations across the two alternatives. Projection onto \(x\) gives the exact two-term disjunctive hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of two compact convex alternatives is obtained by scaled copies of both sets whose nonnegative weights sum to one.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are nonempty compact convex subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed lifted set projects exactly onto \(\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)\).

notation.meaning: nonnegative scalar dilation of the ith convex alternative

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:standard convex-combination formulation for a finite union of compact convex sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For nonempty compact convex sets, the simplex-scaled two-block formulation projects exactly onto the convex hull of their union. The representation kind matches the geometry leaf. The record needs an authoritative disjunctive-programming source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Termwise Validity Certificate for a Two-Term Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed specialization of the finite-union affine-validity test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty sets \(C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), an inequality \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) is valid for \(\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)\) if and only if it is valid for both \(C_1\) and \(C_2\). Equivalently, \[\max\{\sigma_{C_1}(a),\sigma_{C_2}(a)\}\le\beta.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine inequality supports a two-term hull exactly when it is valid on each branch.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1,C_2\) are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Validity on \(\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)\) is equivalent to validity on both terms.
knowledge_statements.title: Termwise Validity Certificate for a Two-Term Hull
