children.title: Factorable-Expression Detection
children.top_down_role: Recognition of expressions admitting factor-based convexification.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity relative to a fixed atom grammar and available domain certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite expression DAG. If operator admission and required domain certificates are checkable in \(O(1)\) time per node, evaluating the recursive factorability predicate once in topological order takes \(O(|V|+|E|)\) time and stores \(O(|V|)\) predicate values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed grammar with constant-time domain checks, recursive factorability detection is linear in graph size.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite expression DAG.
The admitted atom grammar is fixed.
Operator and domain-certificate checks cost \(O(1)\) per node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T(G)=O(|V|+|E|),\qquad S_{\mathrm{aux}}(G)=O(|V|).
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Recursive Factorability Test

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of semantic certification when simplification discards a natural-domain restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The factorable partial expression \(e(x)=x/x\) has domain \(\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\) and graph \[\operatorname{gph}e=\{(x,1):x\ne0\}.\] Replacing it by the everywhere-defined constant \(1\) without retaining \(x\ne0\) yields the different graph \(\{(x,1):x\in\mathbb R\}\). Thus the rewrite is not semantics-preserving.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cancelling x over x without preserving its nonzero-domain condition changes the represented partial function.
assumptions_latex: Expressions include their natural domains.
The proposed rewrite drops the condition \(x\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{gph}(x/x)\ne\operatorname{gph}(1)\text{ when the latter is given domain }\mathbb R.

notation.meaning: Graph of the partial expression e.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Losing Factorability Rewrite

assumptions_latex: The scalar expression is represented by a finite directed acyclic graph.
Leaves are constants or variables; admissible internal nodes are affine sums, products, quotients on nonzero domains, and listed univariate atoms.
Every node carries its natural domain restriction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The root is detected as factorable exactly when every root-to-leaf subgraph satisfies the recursive admissibility predicate.

notation.meaning: Recursive factorability predicate at a node.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Syntactic factorability relative to a declared library of elementary operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F(v)\) recursively. It is true at constant and variable leaves. At an affine-sum node it is true when it is true for every child; at a product or admissible quotient node it is true when it is true for both operands; and at a univariate-atom node \(\phi(u)\) it is true when \(F(u)\) holds and \(u\) lies in the declared domain of \(\phi\). For every other operator set \(F(v)=\mathrm{false}\). The expression is detected as factorable if and only if \(F(r)=\mathrm{true}\) at its root \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expression is detected as factorable when its entire expression graph can be recursively constructed from variables, constants, and an admitted library of elementary operations.
knowledge_statements.title: Factorable-Expression Detection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits, but factorability is relative to a particular atom grammar and domain-certification system. No source establishes that grammar or the claimed exact recursive detector.

children.title: Product-Structure Detection
children.top_down_role: Recognition of bilinear or multilinear product structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Detection complexity on an already canonical expression DAG.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a canonical finite expression DAG \(G=(V,E)\), the predicate that a node has at least two flattened multiplicative factors can be computed in \(O(|V|+|E|)\) time and \(O(|V|)\) auxiliary storage by propagating factor counts capped at two. Materializing every full factor list is output-sensitive and costs \(O(|V|+|E|+L)\), where \(L\) is the total emitted list length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boolean product detection is linear, while full flattened-factor enumeration is output-sensitive.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, acyclic, and canonically normalized.
Operator inspection and capped factor counts have constant cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{detect}}=O(|V|+|E|),\qquad T_{\mathrm{enumerate}}=O(|V|+|E|+L).
knowledge_statements.title: Product Detection and Enumeration Complexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of recovered products by factor type and variable-block dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the recovered factorization be \(e(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(k)})=\prod_{i=1}^k a_i(x^{(i)})\) with pairwise disjoint variable blocks. If every \(a_i\) is linear, then \(e\) is bilinear for \(k=2\) and multilinear for \(k\ge3\). If every \(a_i\) is affine, then \(e\) is biaffine for \(k=2\) and multiaffine for \(k\ge3\), with a bilinear or multilinear highest-order interaction. This certificate does not apply when a factor is nonlinear in its block or the asserted block separation is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Products of linear factors on distinct blocks are bilinear or multilinear; affine factors give the corresponding biaffine or multiaffine structure.
assumptions_latex: The displayed factorization is valid on the modeled domain.
The variable blocks \(x^{(i)}\) are pairwise disjoint.
Each factor is classified as linear or affine in its own block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \prod_{i=1}^k a_i(x^{(i)})\text{ is }k\text{-linear for linear factors and }k\text{-affine for affine factors}.

notation.meaning: Variable block used by factor i.

knowledge_statements.title: Bilinear, Multilinear, and Multiaffine Classification

assumptions_latex: A scalar expression graph has been canonicalized by flattening associative multiplication and removing multiplicative identities.
Each node records its operator and ordered children.
Domain restrictions needed for algebraic simplification are preserved.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure detects a product structure at \(v\) exactly when \(|\mathcal F(v)|\geq2\), and the recovered factors multiply to the subexpression represented by \(v\).

notation.meaning: Canonical multiplicative factors at node v.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Detection of explicit nontrivial products after semantics-preserving canonicalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each node \(v\), define its factor list by \[\mathcal F(v)=\begin{cases}\mathcal F(u_1)\mathbin{\|}\cdots\mathbin{\|}\mathcal F(u_k),&v\text{ is a multiplication node with children }u_1,\ldots,u_k,\\[2pt](v),&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\] where \(\mathbin{\|}\) denotes list concatenation. A nontrivial product is detected at \(v\) precisely when \(|\mathcal F(v)|\geq2\). Canonicalization must guarantee \(e_v=\prod_{u\in\mathcal F(v)}e_u\) on the original domain, so detection does not rely on an invalid cancellation or domain-changing rewrite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After valid canonicalization, a node has product structure precisely when its recursively flattened factor list contains at least two factors.
knowledge_statements.title: Product-Structure Detection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition matches explicit product detection, but exactness depends on the unspecified canonicalization and rewrite semantics. A source for that detection framework is required.

children.title: Expression-Graph Product Recovery
children.top_down_role: Recovery of product structure from nested expression graphs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bottom-up recovery relative to an explicitly declared semantics-preserving normalization system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite expression DAG \(G\), process nodes in topological order, replace children by their canonical representatives, normalize the resulting node using a declared domain-valid rewrite system \(\mathcal R\), and hash-cons identical normalized nodes. The reachable normalized root graph represents the same partial function as \(G\). Report its multiplication nodes with at least two nonconstant factors. The output is complete for products exposed in the chosen \(\mathcal R\)-normal form, not for arbitrary algebraic equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bottom-up normalization and hash-consing recover exactly the products exposed by a declared domain-preserving rewrite system.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite acyclic expression graph.
\(\mathcal R\) is domain-valid and normalization terminates on every processed node.
Canonical representatives preserve the original partial-function semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G'\equiv G\text{ on the recorded domain, and the reported products are exactly those exposed in the }\mathcal R\text{-normal form}.
knowledge_statements.title: Rewrite-Relative Expression-Graph Product Recovery

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional complexity of bottom-up product recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite expression DAG \(G=(V,E)\), the bottom-up recovery pass uses \(O(|V|+|E|)\) expected time and \(O(|V|+|E|)\) space when hash lookup has expected constant cost and normalization performs uniformly bounded work and produces uniformly bounded new representation per node. Termination without bounds on rewrite length or intermediate growth gives no polynomial-time guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recovery is linear under bounded local normalization work; arbitrary terminating rewriting need not be polynomial.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and acyclic.
Hash-consing and lookup have expected constant cost.
Rewrite work and generated representation per input node are uniformly bounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Time Bounded-Local Graph Pass

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on completeness claims for product recovery by normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mathcal R\) is domain-valid, terminating, and confluent, every admitted expression has a unique \(\mathcal R\)-normal form, and normalization recovers exactly the multiplication nodes in that form. This does not recover every product obtainable under a broader algebraic equivalence theory unless \(\mathcal R\) is complete for that theory. For example, without a rule exposing powers, the graph of \(x^2\) need not contain a multiplication node.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unique normal forms make recovery deterministic but do not make the rewrite system complete for unrestricted algebraic equivalence.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal R\) is domain-valid, terminating, and confluent.
Recovery inspects multiplication nodes in the resulting normal form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Recovery is complete for the }\mathcal R\text{-normal form, but not necessarily for broader algebraic equivalence}.
knowledge_statements.title: Rewrite-System Completeness Boundary

assumptions_latex: The input is a finite acyclic expression graph whose nodes are topologically ordered.
Multiplication nodes and semantics-preserving rewrite identities are explicitly declared.
Each rewrite is valid throughout the recorded domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output graph represents the same function on the recorded domain and exposes every product generated by the declared rewrites as a multiplication node.

notation.meaning: Canonical representative associated with node v.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bottom-up recovery of hidden products using a fixed semantics-preserving rewrite library.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a canonicalization table at the leaves. Process each internal node \(v\) in topological order: replace its children by their canonical representatives, apply the declared domain-valid rewrites, flatten nested multiplication nodes, remove multiplicative identities, sort commutative factors, and hash-cons identical results to obtain \(c(v)\). Continue until the root is processed, and output the reachable subgraph \(G'\) rooted at \(c(r)\), together with every multiplication node having at least two nonconstant factors. Stop after the finite topological pass; the output is the recovered graph and its product-node list.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bottom-up canonicalization pass applies valid rewrites, flattens products, and returns an equivalent graph in which recoverable products are explicit.
knowledge_statements.title: Expression-Graph Product Recovery

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the recovery leaf, but a single pass exposes every recoverable product only for a suitably defined terminating and complete normalization system. Those properties and the rewrite library are not sourced.

children.title: Quadratic-Structure Detection
children.top_down_role: Recognition of quadratic forms relevant to convexification.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Structure Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact algebraic detection of scalar quadratic functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Quadratic structure is detected when exact simplification and coefficient collection produce \[f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+q^{\mathsf T}x+r\] with \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\). Equivalently, for a twice continuously differentiable function on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), quadratic structure holds exactly when \(\nabla^2 f(x)=Q\) is constant. Any nonzero residual term of total degree greater than two prevents acceptance. For minimization, the detected quadratic is convex exactly when \(Q\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar function has quadratic structure when it is exactly a polynomial of total degree at most two with a symmetric quadratic coefficient matrix; for a twice continuously differentiable function, this is equivalent to having a constant Hessian. Convexity additionally requires that Hessian to be positive semidefinite.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is represented by an exact arithmetic expression.
The representation permits exact simplification and collection of polynomial coefficients.
Equality tests are exact on the coefficient domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The detector accepts exactly functions representable by polynomials of total degree at most two and returns a symmetric quadratic coefficient matrix \(Q\).

notation.meaning: Symmetric quadratic coefficient matrix and constant Hessian.

children.title: Conic-Structure Detection
children.top_down_role: Recognition of structure admitting conic representation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition relative to a declared grammar of exactly conic-representable atoms; rejection establishes only nonrecognition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a grammar whose primitive graph sets have certified affine conic lifts over a supported cone library. A bottom-up detector may combine these certificates using finite Cartesian products, affine preimages, intersections, and introduction of existential auxiliary coordinates. If it returns \[L=\{(x,z):Ax+Bz+b\in K,\ Cx+Dz=d\}\] and every rewrite is an exact equivalence under verified side conditions, then \(\operatorname{proj}_x L\) equals the set represented by the input expression. Failure to construct such a lift proves only nonrecognition by the selected grammar, not absence of every conic representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact conic atoms and equivalence-preserving composition rules give a sound conic detector. Rejection by its grammar does not prove nonrepresentability.
assumptions_latex: Every primitive atom has a verified exact conic representation.
All domain, sign, and other rewrite side conditions are checked.
The supported library permits the finite product cones used by the construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance supplies an exact affine conic lift, whereas rejection supplies no general nonrepresentability certificate.

notation.meaning: Supported product cone constructed by the detector.
Auxiliary variables introduced by the detector.

knowledge_statements.title: Sound Compositional Conic Detection

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a closed convex set described by finitely many constraints.
The admissible cone library contains specified closed convex cones \(K_i\).
Auxiliary variables may be introduced through affine equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The detector accepts \(S\) exactly when it constructs an affine lift whose projection onto the original variables equals \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conic representability through affine lifting and projection.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 What can be expressed via conic quadratic constraints? p. 85

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Conic structure relative to the library \(\{K_i\}_{i=1}^p\) is detected when the constraints can be transformed, using domain-valid equivalences, into \[S=\left\{x:\exists z,\ A_i x+B_i z+b_i\in K_i\ \text{for }i=1,\ldots,p,\ Cx+Dz=d\right\}.\] Detection is exact only if both inclusions between the original feasible set and this projection are certified. Merely replacing a constraint by an outer conic approximation does not constitute exact conic-structure detection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conic structure is detected when the feasible set is exactly the projection of affine memberships in recognized closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.title: Conic-Structure Detection

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 What can be expressed via conic quadratic constraints? p. 85

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition and exact-lift criterion fit the leaf, but the cited sections concern conic-quadratic representability, whereas the statement quantifies over an arbitrary library of closed convex cones and asserts exact detection. The broader claim needs a matching source.

children.title: Rank-Structure Detection
children.top_down_role: Recognition of matrix rank structure relevant to lifting.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discontinuity of exact rank and threshold dependence of floating-point rank diagnostics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}\), \(\operatorname{rank}M=\#\{i:\sigma_i(M)>0\}\). A numerical rule \(\operatorname{rank}_{\tau}(M)=\#\{i:\sigma_i(M)>\tau\}\) depends on its declared threshold \(\tau\). In particular, \(M_\varepsilon=\operatorname{diag}(1,\varepsilon)\) has exact rank two for every \(\varepsilon>0\), converges to a rank-one matrix as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), and is classified as numerically rank one whenever \(0<\varepsilon\leq\tau<1\). Thus thresholded SVD detection cannot certify an exact algebraic rank bound without exact arithmetic or validated error information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact rank is discontinuous, whereas numerical rank depends on a threshold; treating a small singular value as zero is not an exact rank certificate.
assumptions_latex: Singular values are ordered nonincreasingly.
The numerical-rank threshold satisfies \(\tau\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Thresholded numerical rank is a diagnostic rather than an exact certificate of \(\operatorname{rank}M\leq r\).

notation.meaning: Matrix family approaching a lower-rank limit.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Rank versus Numerical Rank

assumptions_latex: \(M(x)=M_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iM_i\) is an affine matrix map.
A target rank bound \(r\) is specified with \(0\leq r<\min\{p,q\}\).
Matrix dimensions and coefficient arithmetic are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The detector certifies rank structure when the original constraint is equivalent to either the minor system or the stated factorization.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recognition of affine-matrix rank constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rank-bound structure is detected when a constraint can be certified equivalent to \[\operatorname{rank}M(x)\leq r.\] Algebraically, this holds exactly when every \((r+1)\times(r+1)\) minor of \(M(x)\) vanishes. Equivalently, it holds when there exist \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times r}\) and \(V\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times r}\) satisfying \(M(x)=UV^{\mathsf T}\). A detector must distinguish this nonconvex rank constraint from convex surrogates such as a nuclear-norm bound, which do not certify the same feasible set in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine matrix has rank at most r exactly when all larger minors vanish, equivalently when it admits an r-column factorization.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Structure Detection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank, minor, and factorization equivalences are mathematically standard and the condition role fits, but no inspectable source supports this candidate.

children.title: Activation-Disjunction Detection Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Recognition of indicator-controlled convex terms and logical unions.

children.title: Activation-Structure Detection
children.top_down_role: Recognition of indicator-controlled terms or constraint families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-independent semantic test for a binary activation structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\{0,1\}\) and define \(S_i=\{x:(x,i)\in S\}\). For a prescribed inactive point \(x^0\), \(S\) has binary activation semantics with active set \(C\) if and only if \[S_0=\{x^0\},\qquad S_1=C.\] Syntactic occurrence of an indicator or valid on-off bounds alone need not establish the second equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary activation is certified by verifying that the two indicator fibers equal the prescribed inactive singleton and intended active set.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\{0,1\}\) is the controlled feasible set.
\(x^0\) is the prescribed inactive value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ has the stated activation semantics}\iff S_0=\{x^0\}\text{ and }S_1=C.

notation.meaning: Feasible fiber at indicator value i.

knowledge_statements.title: Fiber Certificate for Binary Activation
Activation-Structure Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition of a bounded binary on-off variable pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bounded activation pattern is detected when the model contains, explicitly or after valid propagation, \[\ell_i y\leq x_i\leq u_i y\qquad(i=1,\ldots,n),\quad y\in\{0,1\}.\] These inequalities force \(x=0\) when \(y=0\) and impose \(\ell\leq x\leq u\) when \(y=1\). They identify the on-off bounds but do not by themselves certify that the box is the complete active-state feasible set. More generally, activation detection must identify the indicator, its active and inactive conventions, and every variable controlled by it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary activation bounds are detected when they force controlled variables to zero in the inactive state and impose valid componentwise bounds in the active state; other active-state constraints may still apply.
assumptions_latex: \(y\in\{0,1\}\) is a binary indicator and \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a controlled variable.
Finite componentwise vectors \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfy \(\ell\leq u\) and give valid bounds in the active state.
The intended inactive state fixes \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequalities certify that \(y=0\) forces \(x=0\) and that \(y=1\) imposes the valid bounds \(\ell\leq x\leq u\).

children.title: Disjunction-Structure Detection
children.top_down_role: Recognition of logical unions suitable for disjunctive reformulation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case branch count when Boolean normalization fixes one complete assignment per branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\ge1\), the odd-parity condition \(z_1\oplus\cdots\oplus z_m=1\) on \(z\in\{0,1\}^m\) has \(2^{m-1}\) satisfying assignments. Therefore an exact normalization in which every branch fixes one complete assignment has \(2^{m-1}\) nonempty branches, although the parity predicate has a linear-size XOR description.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assignment-level disjunctive normalization can be exponentially larger than the Boolean predicate being normalized.
assumptions_latex: Each normalized branch fixes all Boolean variables to one assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K=2^{m-1}\text{ nonempty branches are required for odd parity under assignment-level enumeration}.
knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Assignment-Branch Enumeration Boundary

assumptions_latex: Each branch set \(S_k\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is explicitly described and nonempty.
The feasible condition is a finite Boolean formula over branch-membership predicates.
Logical normalization preserves the original variable domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The detector accepts exactly when the feasible set is certified as a finite union of the recovered branch sets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-union detection after domain-preserving logical normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Disjunctive structure is detected when logical normalization yields \[x\in S=\bigcup_{k=1}^K S_k,\] equivalently \((x\in S_1)\lor\cdots\lor(x\in S_K)\), for finite \(K\geq2\). The recovered branches must satisfy equality with the original feasible condition, not merely cover it. Intersections inside a branch are retained as part of that branch description, and shared constraints may be factored outside the disjunction without changing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model has disjunctive structure when its feasible condition is exactly a finite union of explicitly recovered branch sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Disjunction-Structure Detection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-union condition is precise, agrees with the plain statement, and fits the detection leaf, but it has no inspectable source.

children.title: Activation-to-Disjunction Translation
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between activation patterns and logical unions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact two-branch translation when either binary state may have a non-singleton feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C_0,C_1\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(y\in\{0,1\}\), \[\{(x,y):y=0\Rightarrow x\in C_0,\ y=1\Rightarrow x\in C_1\}=(C_0\times\{0\})\cup(C_1\times\{1\}).\] No convexity, boundedness, or closedness assumption is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary state-dependent feasible set is exactly the union of its state-zero and state-one branches.
assumptions_latex: \(C_0,C_1\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{(x,y):y=0\Rightarrow x\in C_0,\ y=1\Rightarrow x\in C_1\}=(C_0\times\{0\})\cup(C_1\times\{1\}).

notation.meaning: Feasible sets in the two states.

knowledge_statements.title: General Two-State Activation Translation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Categorical and one-hot extension of activation-to-disjunction translation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). For a state variable \(j\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\), the condition \(x\in C_j\) is exactly \[\bigcup_{k=1}^K(C_k\times\{k\}).\] Equivalently, for a one-hot vector \(y\in\{0,1\}^K\) with \(\sum_k y_k=1\), it is \[\bigcup_{k=1}^K(C_k\times\{e_k\}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite categorical or one-hot activation is exactly a finite disjunction indexed by its states.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is finite and positive.
\(C_k\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) for each state.
In the one-hot form, \(y\in\{0,1\}^K\) and \(\sum_k y_k=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{(x,j):x\in C_j\}=\bigcup_{k=1}^K(C_k\times\{k\}).

notation.meaning: k-th coordinate vector encoding state k.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-State Activation Translation

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is the active-state feasible set and \(0\) is the prescribed inactive point.
\(y\in\{0,1\}\) is the activation indicator.
The activation semantics are \(y=0\Rightarrow x=0\) and \(y=1\Rightarrow x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The activation formulation and the two-branch disjunction define exactly the same feasible pairs \((x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact set-theoretic translation of binary activation into two disjunctive branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The binary activation semantics have the exact disjunctive representation \[\{(x,y):y\in\{0,1\},\ y=0\Rightarrow x=0,\ y=1\Rightarrow x\in C\}=\bigl(\{0\}\times\{0\}\bigr)\cup\bigl(C\times\{1\}\bigr).\] Hence activation detection supplies two branches: the inactive branch \((x,y)=(0,0)\) and the active branch \(x\in C,\ y=1\). Any subsequent convex-hull or big-\(M\) formulation is exact only under its own additional hypotheses; the set-theoretic translation itself requires none.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary on-off constraint is exactly the union of an inactive singleton branch and the active feasible-set branch.
knowledge_statements.title: Activation-to-Disjunction Translation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set-theoretic translation is exact and representation is the correct content kind, but no cited source supports the record.

children.title: Representation Selection
children.top_down_role: Choice among mathematically equivalent or systematically ordered convex formulations.

children.title: Native Conic versus Polyhedral Approximation
children.top_down_role: Selection between direct cone support and linear outer approximation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Impossibility of an exact finite linear representation or finite polyhedral lift for a nonpolyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite system of linear equalities and inequalities defines a polyhedron, and every finite-dimensional linear projection of a polyhedron is polyhedral. Consequently, if a closed convex cone \(K\) is nonpolyhedral, it has neither a finite exact linear-inequality description in its native space nor a finite polyhedral extended formulation whose projection is \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A genuinely nonpolyhedral cone cannot be represented exactly by finitely many linear constraints, even through a finite polyhedral lift.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a finite-dimensional closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\text{ nonpolyhedral}\Rightarrow K\) has no finite polyhedral extended formulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Exact Polyhedral Representation Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value and minimizer convergence for nested polyhedral outer approximations on a common compact domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be compact, let \(A:X\to\mathbb R^d\) and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, and let \(K\subseteq P_{t+1}\subseteq P_t\) be closed sets with each \(P_t\) polyhedral and \(\bigcap_{t\geq1}P_t=K\). Define \[F=\{x\in X:A(x)\in K\},\qquad F_t=\{x\in X:A(x)\in P_t\},\] and assume \(F\neq\varnothing\). For minimization, \(p_t=\min_{F_t}f\) satisfies \(p_t\leq p_{t+1}\leq p^*=\min_Ff\) and \(p_t\uparrow p^*\). Every accumulation point of minimizers from \(F_t\) is a native-feasible minimizer. For maximization, the corresponding relaxed upper values decrease to the native optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested polyhedral outer approximations give monotone bounds converging to the native conic optimum on a common compact domain.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is compact.
\(A\) and \(f\) are continuous.
\(K\subseteq P_{t+1}\subseteq P_t\), every \(P_t\) is closed and polyhedral, and \(\bigcap_tP_t=K\).
\(F\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_t\uparrow p^*\) for minimization, with every minimizer accumulation point in \(\operatorname*{argmin}_F f\).

notation.meaning: Polyhedral outer approximation at refinement t.
Continuous map into the cone space.

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Polyhedral Outer-Approximation Convergence

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is a closed convex cone and \(P_t\supseteq K\) are closed polyhedral outer approximations.
The problem minimizes a linear objective over affine constraints and membership in \(K\).
For convergence, the relevant relaxed feasible region is compact and \(P_{t+1}\subseteq P_t\) with \(\bigcap_tP_t=K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Native conic representation preserves the exact feasible set; polyhedral outer approximation gives lower bounds that increase to the conic optimum under the stated nestedness and compactness assumptions.

notation.meaning: Polyhedral outer approximation at refinement t.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact native cone use versus nested linear outer approximation in minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p^*\) be the minimum with native constraint \(s(x)\in K\), and let \(p_t\) replace it by \(s(x)\in P_t\). Since \(K\subseteq P_t\), every native-feasible point is relaxed-feasible, so \(p_t\leq p^*\). Nested refinement gives \(p_t\leq p_{t+1}\leq p^*\). If the relevant relaxed feasible region is compact and \(\bigcap_{t=1}^{\infty}P_t=K\), then every accumulation point of relaxed minimizers is native-feasible and \(p_t\uparrow p^*\). Native cone support avoids approximation error and should be selected when the solver supports \(K\) reliably.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Native cone support is exact. Polyhedral outer approximations yield lower bounds for minimization and converge under nested refinement, exact intersection, and compactness.
knowledge_statements.title: Native Conic versus Polyhedral Approximation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits the selection topic and the convergence claim is standard under a common compact relaxed feasible region, but the cited conic-quadratic sections do not specifically support nested polyhedral convergence. The map s used in the statement is also not introduced in the assumptions or notation.

children.title: Compact versus Extended Formulations
children.top_down_role: Selection between smaller original-space models and stronger or more structured lifted models.

knowledge_statements.title: Compact versus Extended Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional comparison through projection onto the original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the compact feasible set be \(F=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g_i(x)\leq 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\). An extended formulation is a set \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) satisfying \(F=\operatorname{proj}_x Q=\{x:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^p,\ (x,y)\in Q\}\). For every objective \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the formulations then have equal values: \[\inf_{x\in F}c^\top x=\inf_{(x,y)\in Q}c^\top x.\] The extended formulation may contain more variables and constraints while providing simpler cones, stronger accessible relaxations, or more exploitable sparsity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted model is equivalent to a compact model when projecting out its auxiliary variables recovers exactly the original feasible set and preserves every original-variable linear objective value.
assumptions_latex: \(F\neq\varnothing\) and \(Q\neq\varnothing\).
The objective depends only on \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\operatorname{proj}_xQ\) and \(\inf_{x\in F}c^\top x=\inf_{(x,y)\in Q}c^\top x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Extension Does Not Imply Computational Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absence of a universal size or structural advantage for exact extensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any nonempty \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(p\geq1\), define \(Q=F\times\{0\}^p\). Then \(\operatorname{proj}_xQ=F\), but the extension merely adds \(p\) auxiliary variables and the equations \(y=0\) without simplifying the description of \(F\). Hence projection equivalence alone implies no reduction in formulation size or descriptive complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact extension can consist entirely of redundant variables, so exactness alone does not make it preferable to a compact formulation.
assumptions_latex: \(F\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(F\times\{0\}^p)=F\), yet the extension need not reduce formulation size or descriptive complexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Extension Does Not Imply Computational Dominance

children.title: Static versus Dynamic Strengthening
children.top_down_role: Selection between initial reformulation and iterative separation or domain reduction.

knowledge_statements.title: Static versus Dynamic Strengthening
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of upfront constraints with iterative valid-inequality separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_0\supseteq F\) be an initial relaxation. Static strengthening selects a valid family \(\mathcal C\) before optimization and solves over \(R_{\mathrm{stat}}=R_0\cap\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal C}C\). Dynamic strengthening generates valid sets \(C_k\supseteq F\) from current iterates and forms \(R_{k+1}=R_k\cap C_k\). Every dynamic iterate remains an outer relaxation. If the generated family is finite and eventually equals \(\mathcal C\), then the terminal dynamic and static feasible regions coincide; otherwise dynamic strengthening trades finite initial size for repeated separation and reoptimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Static strengthening installs valid constraints initially; dynamic strengthening adds them iteratively. Both remain valid relaxations, and they coincide when the dynamic process eventually generates the same family.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq R_0\).
Every selected or generated set \(C\) contains \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq R_{k+1}\subseteq R_k\), and generation of all \(C\in\mathcal C\) gives \(R_k=R_{\mathrm{stat}}\).

notation.meaning: Relaxation after k dynamic strengthening steps.
Static family of valid constraint sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite exactness of dynamic strengthening for an infinite target family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let R_\infty=R_0\cap\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal C}C and let each iteration add finitely many members of the infinite family \mathcal C. After k iterations, R_k=R_0\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^k C_i. Equality R_k=R_\infty at a finite k requires the generated finite subfamily to define R_\infty relative to R_0; separation of some violated member at every nonterminal iterate does not ensure that such a finite subfamily exists. For R_0=\mathbb R^2, the Euclidean unit disk is the intersection of all its supporting halfspaces, whereas every finite subcollection defines a polyhedron strictly containing the disk.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separation oracle does not guarantee finite exact termination. The unit disk has no exact finite description using its supporting halfspaces.
assumptions_latex: R_\infty=R_0\cap\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal C}C with \mathcal C infinite.
Each iteration adds only finitely many members of \mathcal C.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_k=R_\infty\text{ for finite }k\Longrightarrow R_\infty=R_0\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^k C_i.

notation.meaning: Relaxation defined by the complete family.
Relaxation after finitely many generated constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Family Finite-Termination Boundary

children.title: Reformulation-Relaxation Validation System
children.top_down_role: Checks for projection equivalence, relaxation validity, exactness, and bound certification.

children.title: Projection-Equivalence Validation
children.top_down_role: Validation that auxiliary-variable reformulations preserve the intended original-space feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Equivalence Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-inclusion certificate for an auxiliary-variable reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an intended feasible set \(F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and lifted set \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\), projection equivalence holds exactly when both conditions are valid: \[\forall x\in F\ \exists y\in\mathbb{R}^p:(x,y)\in Q,\qquad \forall(x,y)\in Q:x\in F.\] The first condition certifies that no intended feasible point is lost; the second certifies that the lift introduces no spurious projected point. Together they are a directly checkable logical certificate of \(\operatorname{proj}_xQ=F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted reformulation is projection-equivalent precisely when every original feasible point has a lift and every lifted feasible point projects to an original feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_xQ=F\).

notation.meaning: Projection of Q onto its original-variable coordinates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent projection-equality test for nonempty closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) and \(S=\operatorname{proj}_xQ\) be nonempty closed convex subsets of a finite-dimensional space. Then \[F=S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sigma_F(c)=\sigma_S(c)\ \text{for every }c,\] where \(\sigma_C(c)=\sup_{x\in C}c^\top x\) may be extended-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonempty closed convex sets, equality of every linear support value is equivalent to projection equivalence.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(\operatorname{proj}_xQ\) are nonempty, closed, and convex.
The ambient space is finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\operatorname{proj}_xQ\iff \sigma_F=\sigma_{\operatorname{proj}_xQ}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Function Certificate under Closed Convexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Objective Agreement Can Identify Only a Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of objective-value validation without closed-convex assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{-1,1\}\) and \(S=[-1,1]\). For every \(c\in\mathbb R\), \[\inf_{x\in F}cx=\inf_{x\in S}cx=-|c|\quad\text{and}\quad\sup_{x\in F}cx=\sup_{x\in S}cx=|c|,\] yet \(F\neq S\). Thus even agreement for every linear objective does not certify set equality for arbitrary nonconvex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All linear optimization values can agree while the represented feasible sets differ, because linear objectives see only the closed convex hull.
assumptions_latex: No convexity assumption is imposed on the intended set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_F=\sigma_S\) but \(F\neq S\).
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Objective Agreement Can Identify Only a Convex Hull

children.title: Outer-Relaxation Validity Validation
children.top_down_role: Validation that every intended feasible point remains represented by the relaxation.

knowledge_statements.title: Outer-Relaxation Validity Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible-point retention certificate for original-space or lifted relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be the intended feasible set and let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\). An original-space set \(R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a valid outer relaxation exactly when \(F\subseteq R\). A lifted set \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) is a valid outer relaxation exactly when \(F\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_xQ\), equivalently, when \(\forall x\in F\ \exists y\in\mathbb{R}^p\) such that \((x,y)\in Q\). For minimization with the same original-variable objective, define \(v_F=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\), \(v_R=\inf_{x\in R}f(x)\), and \(v_Q=\inf_{(x,y)\in Q}f(x)\). Then \(F\subseteq R\) implies \(v_R\leq v_F\), while \(F\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_xQ\) implies \(v_Q\leq v_F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer-relaxation validity means retaining every intended feasible point, directly or through a lift. With the same original-variable objective, either valid relaxation supplies a minimization lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(F\neq\varnothing\).
The relaxation uses the same objective \(f(x)\) as the original problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq R\Rightarrow v_R\leq v_F\), and \(F\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_xQ\Rightarrow v_Q\leq v_F\).

notation.meaning: Original, original-space relaxation, and lifted-relaxation infimum values.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of Feasible-Point Retention Destroys the Bound Guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the minimization lower-bound conclusion without outer containment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{0,1\}\), \(R=\{1\}\), and \(f(x)=x\). Then \(F\nsubseteq R\), while \(\inf_{x\in F}f(x)=0<1=\inf_{x\in R}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A purported relaxation that removes intended feasible points need not provide a minimization lower bound.
assumptions_latex: The same objective is used on \(F\) and \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\nsubseteq R\) and \(v_R>v_F\).

notation.meaning: Original and purported relaxed feasible sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Feasible-Point Retention Destroys the Bound Guarantee

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective Consistency Is Required for Lifted Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection containment alone does not compare values when the lifted objective differs from the original objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{0\}\), \(Q=\{(0,0)\}\), and let the original objective be \(f(0)=0\). Although \(F=\operatorname{proj}_xQ\), assigning the lifted minimization objective \(h(0,0)=1\) gives lifted value one, which is not a lower bound on the original value zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even exact projected feasibility does not yield the expected value bound if the lifted objective is inconsistent with the original objective.
assumptions_latex: The lifted objective is not required to equal or fiber-represent the original objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\operatorname{proj}_xQ\) but \(\inf_Q h>\inf_F f\).
knowledge_statements.title: Objective Consistency Is Required for Lifted Bounds

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bound direction supplied by a valid outer relaxation in maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\subseteq R\), then for the same objective \(f\), \[\sup_{x\in F}f(x)\leq\sup_{x\in R}f(x).\] Likewise, if \(F\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_xQ\) and the lifted objective is \(f(x)\), then \[\sup_{x\in F}f(x)\leq\sup_{(x,y)\in Q}f(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid outer relaxation supplies an upper bound for maximization.
assumptions_latex: The original and relaxed models use the same original-variable objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq R\Rightarrow w_F\leq w_R\), and \(F\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_xQ\Rightarrow w_F\leq w_Q\).
knowledge_statements.title: Maximization Upper-Bound Consequence

children.title: Exactness-Gap Diagnostic System
children.top_down_role: Diagnostics distinguishing exact reformulations from useful but inexact relaxations.

children.title: Exactness Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Evidence used to assess whether a reformulation preserves the target value.

knowledge_statements.title: Exactness Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value and optimizer-recovery tests for a minimization relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(f:R\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) have attained finite minima \(v_F\) and \(v_R\). The relaxation is value-exact when \(v_R=v_F\). It is solution-exact when it has an optimizer \(x_R\in F\); such an optimizer satisfies \(f(x_R)=v_F\) and certifies value exactness. For a lifted relaxation \(Q\), replace \(x_R\in F\) by existence of an optimal \((x_R,y_R)\in Q\) whose projection satisfies \(x_R\in F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exactness is diagnosed by equality of optimal values; an optimal relaxed point that is feasible for the original problem additionally certifies recoverability of an original optimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq R\).
Both minimum values are finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_R\in F\) and \(f(x_R)=v_R\) imply \(v_R=v_F\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Value Gap Does Not Certify Universal Optimizer Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of value exactness, existential recovery, and recovery of every relaxed optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{0\}\), \(R=[0,1]\), and \(f(x)=0\) on \(R\). Then both minimum values equal zero and \(x=0\) is a recoverable relaxed optimizer, but every \(x\in(0,1]\) is also a relaxed optimizer and is not originally feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero gap and one recoverable relaxed optimizer do not ensure that every relaxed optimizer is originally feasible.
assumptions_latex: The original and relaxed minima are attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_R=v_F\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{R}f\cap F\neq\varnothing\), but \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{R}f\nsubseteq F\).
knowledge_statements.title: Zero Value Gap Does Not Certify Universal Optimizer Recovery

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value exactness does not require attainment, whereas optimizer-recovery diagnostics do.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F\subseteq R\), finite equality \(\inf_{x\in F}f(x)=\inf_{x\in R}f(x)\) defines value exactness without requiring either infimum to be attained. An optimizer-recovery certificate requires an attained relaxed optimum lying in \(F\). For example, with \(F=R=(0,1)\) and \(f(x)=x\), the relaxation is value-exact with common infimum zero but has no optimizer to recover.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Value exactness can hold without attained optima, but optimizer recovery requires an actual relaxed optimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq R\).
Both infimum values are finite for the value-exactness statement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_R=v_F\) does not imply \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{R}f\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Attainment Boundary for Exactness Diagnostics

children.title: Relaxation-Gap Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Assessment of value separation introduced by an inexact relaxation.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Gap Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute and scale-normalized gaps for minimization relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a valid minimization relaxation with finite values \(v_R\leq v_F\), define the absolute gap by \(g_{\mathrm{abs}}=v_F-v_R\geq0\). Given a fixed scale \(s>0\), define the normalized gap by \(g_s=(v_F-v_R)/s\). A common data-dependent choice is \(s=\max\{1,|v_F|\}\). Adding the same constant to both objective functions leaves \(g_{\mathrm{abs}}\) unchanged, while multiplying both objectives by a positive scalar multiplies \(g_{\mathrm{abs}}\) by that scalar. Zero absolute gap is equivalent to value exactness, although it need not imply that every relaxation optimizer is originally feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relaxation gap is the original value minus the relaxed lower bound. It is unchanged by a common additive objective shift. A zero gap gives value exactness but does not ensure every relaxed optimizer is recoverable.
assumptions_latex: \(v_R\leq v_F\) are finite minimization values.
\(s>0\) is fixed for normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_{\mathrm{abs}}\geq0\), and \(g_{\mathrm{abs}}=0\iff v_R=v_F\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign-correct gap diagnostic for valid maximization relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a valid maximization relaxation with finite values \(w_F\leq w_R\), define \(g_{\max}=w_R-w_F\geq0\). For any fixed \(s>0\), \(g_{\max}/s\) is a normalized gap. A common additive objective shift leaves \(g_{\max}\) unchanged, positive objective scaling scales it equally, and \(g_{\max}=0\) is equivalent to value exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For maximization, the relaxation gap is the relaxed upper value minus the original value.
assumptions_latex: \(w_F\leq w_R\) are finite maximization values.
\(s>0\) for normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_{\max}=w_R-w_F\geq0\), with \(g_{\max}=0\iff w_R=w_F\).
knowledge_statements.title: Maximization Relaxation-Gap Convention

children.title: Inexactness Boundary Identification
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes associated with loss of exactness.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexactness Boundary Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter-space boundary separating exact and positively gapped instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a parameterized family with finite original and relaxed minimization values \(v_F(\theta)\) and \(v_R(\theta)\), define \(g(\theta)=v_F(\theta)-v_R(\theta)\geq0\). The exactness region is \(E=\{\theta:g(\theta)=0\}\), and the inexactness region is \(I=\{\theta:g(\theta)>0\}\). A transition point belongs to the inexactness boundary when \[\theta\in\partial I=\overline I\cap\overline{\Theta\setminus I}.\] If \(g\) is continuous, every such boundary point satisfies \(g(\theta)=0\), while arbitrarily nearby parameters in \(I\) have positive gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inexactness boundary consists of parameter values approached by both positively gapped and non-gapped instances; continuity forces zero gap at the transition itself.
assumptions_latex: \(\Theta\) is a topological parameter space.
\(g:\Theta\to\mathbb{R}_+\) is continuous for the stated boundary conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta\in\partial I\Rightarrow g(\theta)=0\) and every neighborhood of \(\theta\) meets \(I\).

source_refs.locator: 3.4.2 The geometry of a max-cut relaxation p. 58

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4.2 The geometry of a max-cut relaxation p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuity Is Essential for Zero Gap on the Inexactness Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the zero-gap boundary conclusion for a discontinuous parameterized gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Theta=\mathbb R\), with original values \(v_F(0)=1\), \(v_F(\theta)=0\) for \(\theta\neq0\), and relaxed values \(v_R(\theta)=0\) for every \(\theta\). Then \(g=v_F-v_R\) has \(I=\{\theta:g(\theta)>0\}=\{0\}\). Hence \(0\in\partial I\), but \(g(0)=1>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without continuity, an inexactness-boundary point can itself have a positive gap.
assumptions_latex: The finite value functions are not assumed continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\partial\{\theta:g(\theta)>0\}\) and \(g(0)>0\).

notation.meaning: Parameter region with positive relaxation gap.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuity Is Essential for Zero Gap on the Inexactness Boundary

children.title: Numerical-Structural Failure Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Implementation failures that may persist even when the underlying convexification is mathematically valid.

children.title: Scaling-Degeneracy Failure Coupling
children.top_down_role: Numerical degradation caused by incompatible magnitudes, redundant structure, and near-degenerate constraints.

children.title: Poor Numerical Scaling
children.top_down_role: Degradation associated with incompatible coefficient or variable magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Poor Numerical Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent equality systems can have arbitrarily different coefficient conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\varepsilon\leq1\), consider \[A_\varepsilon x=b_\varepsilon,\qquad A_\varepsilon=\operatorname{diag}(1,\varepsilon),\qquad b_\varepsilon=(1,\varepsilon)^\top.\] Every member has the same singleton feasible set \(\{(1,1)^\top\}\), but its spectral condition number is \(\kappa_2(A_\varepsilon)=1/\varepsilon\). Thus equivalent row scaling can make coefficient conditioning arbitrarily poor as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). In floating-point computation, the small row may become ineffective relative to feasibility tolerances or rounding error even though the exact feasible set is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Row scaling can leave the exact feasible set unchanged while making the coefficient condition number arbitrarily large and a constraint numerically ineffective.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\varepsilon\leq1\).
Conditioning is measured in the matrix spectral norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{feas}(A_\varepsilon,b_\varepsilon)=\{(1,1)^\top\}\) while \(\kappa_2(A_\varepsilon)\to\infty\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal equilibration as an equivalent representation with explicit primal and multiplier recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Ax=b\), choose nonsingular diagonal matrices \(D_r\) and \(D_c\), set \(x=D_cy\), and solve \[(D_rAD_c)y=D_rb.\] The systems are exactly equivalent, with recovery \(x=D_cy\). If \(\lambda'\) multiplies the transformed equality \(D_r(AD_cy-b)=0\), then the corresponding original multiplier is \(\lambda=D_r^{\mathsf T}\lambda'\). Diagonal equilibration may reduce coefficient disparities, but nonsingular scaling cannot change exact rank or repair structural rank deficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonsingular diagonal row and variable scaling preserves an equality system under explicit primal and multiplier recovery maps, but cannot cure exact rank deficiency.
assumptions_latex: \(D_r\) and \(D_c\) are nonsingular diagonal matrices.
Primal and multiplier quantities are mapped back before interpretation in original units.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scaled and original systems are equivalent, while exact rank deficiency is invariant under the scaling.
knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent Row and Variable Rescaling

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Tolerances Depend on Constraint Units
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why feasibility residuals must be interpreted in original or explicitly normalized units.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replacing a scalar equality \(r(x)=0\) by \(\alpha r(x)=0\), \(\alpha>0\), preserves its exact zero set. Under a fixed absolute stopping test, however, \(|\alpha r(x)|\leq\varepsilon\) is equivalent to \(|r(x)|\leq\varepsilon/\alpha\). Arbitrary row scaling can therefore make the same original residual appear arbitrarily accurate or inaccurate. A scale-aware feasibility certificate must map residuals back to original units or use declared relative normalizations with nonzero reference scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact feasibility is invariant under positive row scaling, but a fixed absolute residual tolerance is not; residuals must be unscaled or explicitly normalized.
assumptions_latex: The numerical test uses a fixed absolute tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A fixed absolute residual threshold has no scaling-invariant meaning without recovery to original units or declared normalization.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Tolerances Depend on Constraint Units

children.title: Constraint Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Degradation associated with redundant or nearly dependent constraint structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LICQ degeneracy for smooth finite-dimensional constraint systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(F=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:h_j(x)=0,\ j=1,\ldots,p,\ g_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), where all constraints are continuously differentiable. At \(\bar x\in F\), let \(I(\bar x)=\{i:g_i(\bar x)=0\}\). The system is constraint-degenerate at \(\bar x\) in the linear-independence-constraint-qualification sense when \[\{\nabla h_j(\bar x):1\leq j\leq p\}\cup\{\nabla g_i(\bar x):i\in I(\bar x)\}\] is linearly dependent. Otherwise LICQ holds at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth constraint system is LICQ-degenerate at a feasible point when the equality gradients and active inequality gradients are linearly dependent.
assumptions_latex: Each \(h_j\) and \(g_i\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
\(\bar x\in F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degeneracy at \(\bar x\) is equivalent to linear dependence of the equality and active-inequality gradients.

notation.meaning: Active inequality index set at the feasible point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Duplicate equalities show that LICQ failure may be purely representational.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The system \[x=0,\qquad 2x=0\] has the singleton feasible set \(\{0\}\), but its equality gradients \(1\) and \(2\) are linearly dependent, so LICQ fails at its only feasible point. Removing either equality preserves the feasible set and restores LICQ. Thus redundant representation alone can create LICQ degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicating an equality can create LICQ degeneracy without changing the feasible set.
assumptions_latex: The variable is scalar and both constraints are smooth equalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: LICQ failure need not imply geometric ambiguity or ill-posedness of the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Constraints without Geometric Ill-Posedness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The local multiplier consequence of LICQ and the limited implications of its failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a feasible point \(\bar x\), suppose KKT stationarity holds with multipliers \((\lambda,\mu_I)\) for the equality and active inequality constraints. If LICQ holds, these active multipliers are unique. If LICQ fails, uniqueness is no longer guaranteed, but multipliers may still exist and the point may still be optimal under a weaker constraint qualification. Thus active-gradient dependence diagnoses LICQ degeneracy; by itself it proves neither infeasibility, nonoptimality, nor failure of every constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LICQ makes active KKT multipliers unique. Its failure removes that guarantee but does not itself imply infeasibility, nonoptimality, or absence of multipliers.
assumptions_latex: The constraints are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
KKT stationarity holds at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: LICQ implies uniqueness of active KKT multipliers; failure of LICQ alone has none of the stronger stated consequences.
knowledge_statements.title: LICQ and Multiplier Uniqueness

children.title: Scaling–Degeneracy Interaction
children.top_down_role: Failure regimes where scaling defects amplify near-degenerate structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling–Degeneracy Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact rank invariance versus finite-precision detectability under row scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n}\) collect equality and active-constraint gradients, and let \(D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_r)\) with every \(d_i>0\). Then \(\operatorname{rank}(DG)=\operatorname{rank}(G)\), so positive row scaling cannot create or remove exact LICQ degeneracy. Nevertheless, \[d_{\min}\sigma_{\min}(G)\leq\sigma_{\min}(DG)\leq d_{\max}\sigma_{\min}(G),\] with analogous bounds for the largest singular value. Large scaling disparities can therefore change numerical rank decisions and amplify the apparent severity of near-degeneracy under fixed floating-point tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive scaling preserves exact constraint degeneracy but can greatly alter singular values, numerical rank tests, and the apparent severity of near-degeneracy.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is the active-gradient matrix.
\(0<d_{\min}\leq d_i\leq d_{\max}<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(DG)=\operatorname{rank}(G)\), although numerical rank may change under a fixed tolerance.

notation.meaning: Matrix of active constraint gradients as rows.

children.title: Oversized or Dense Lifted Models
children.top_down_role: Computational failure caused by excessive auxiliary dimension, fill-in, or constraint density.

knowledge_statements.title: Oversized or Dense Lifted Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense direct linear-algebra cost of an auxiliary-variable lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a lifted formulation has \(N=n+p\) primal variables after adding \(p\) auxiliaries, and an iteration of a Newton-type method forms and factors a dense \(N\times N\) symmetric positive-definite system. Classical dense Cholesky factorization requires \(N^3/3+O(N^2)\) arithmetic operations and \(N(N+1)/2\) stored scalars. Hence the per-factorization time is \(O((n+p)^3)\) and memory is \(O((n+p)^2)\). A lift can therefore be computationally inferior despite strengthening the relaxation when it destroys sparsity or makes \(p\) dominant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense lift with many auxiliary variables can raise direct Newton-system factorization to cubic time and quadratic memory in the total lifted dimension.
assumptions_latex: A dense direct Cholesky factorization is used.
The Newton system has dimension \(N=n+p\) and is positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Time is \(O((n+p)^3)\) and storage is \(O((n+p)^2)\) per dense factorization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fill-In Boundary for Lifted Linear Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symbolic fill caused by eliminating a sparse lifted Newton or KKT system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a sparse symmetric positive-definite matrix and fix an elimination ordering. Eliminating a vertex joins all of its later neighbors, and the resulting chordal completion determines the symbolic nonzero pattern of its Cholesky factor. For example, a star sparsity graph has \(O(N)\) edges, but eliminating its center first makes its \(N-1\) leaves a clique and produces \(\Theta(N^2)\) factor nonzeros. Thus a sparse lifted system can require quadratic factor storage and dense-order arithmetic under an unfavorable lifted graph or ordering; explicit model nonzeros alone do not predict factorization cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparse lifted system can factor densely because elimination creates fill; explicit model nonzeros alone do not predict direct-solver cost.
assumptions_latex: A direct Cholesky-type factorization is applied to a symmetric positive-definite system.
An elimination ordering is fixed.
Symbolic fill is not removed through accidental numerical cancellation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A lifted system with \(O(N)\) explicit sparsity can have \(\Theta(N^2)\) factor storage, so assessment must include the elimination graph and predicted fill.
knowledge_statements.title: Fill-In Boundary for Lifted Linear Systems

children.title: Weak or Missing Domains
children.top_down_role: Geometric and numerical weakness inherited from absent or overly broad bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak or Missing Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: McCormick-relaxation weakness caused by broad or absent variable bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z=xy\) on \(0\leq x,y\leq U\), the McCormick outer relaxation is \[z\geq0,\quad z\geq Ux+Uy-U^2,\quad z\leq Ux,\quad z\leq Uy.\] At \(x=y=U/2\), it permits every \(z\in[0,U^2/2]\), whereas the nonlinear graph requires \(z=U^2/4\). Thus the maximum vertical discrepancy at that point is \(U^2/4\) and grows quadratically with the domain width. With no finite bounds, these finite McCormick inequalities cannot be instantiated, demonstrating how missing domains can eliminate this convexification mechanism entirely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Broad bounds make a bilinear McCormick relaxation increasingly weak, while absent finite bounds prevent the usual finite envelope inequalities from being formed.
assumptions_latex: The bilinear graph is restricted to \([0,U]^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum permitted discrepancy from \(z=xy\) at \((x,y)=(U/2,U/2)\) is \(U^2/4\).

notation.meaning: Lifted variable representing the product xy.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of bilinear McCormick-envelope error on both factor-domain widths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z=xy\) on \([\ell_x,u_x]\times[\ell_y,u_y]\), let \(\Delta_x=u_x-\ell_x\) and \(\Delta_y=u_y-\ell_y\). At the box midpoint, the McCormick relaxation permits values from \(xy-\Delta_x\Delta_y/4\) to \(xy+\Delta_x\Delta_y/4\). Thus its maximum upward or downward discrepancy there is \(\Delta_x\Delta_y/4\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the midpoint of a rectangular factor domain, McCormick error scales as the product of the two domain widths.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_x<u_x\) and \(\ell_y<u_y\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max |z-xy|=\Delta_x\Delta_y/4\) at the box midpoint over the permitted McCormick interval.

notation.meaning: Widths of the two factor domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Rectangular-Domain McCormick Discrepancy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonic Strengthening by Valid Domain Tightening
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of tighter valid factor bounds on a bilinear McCormick relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B'\subseteq B\) be finite rectangular domains, and let \(M(B)\) denote the McCormick relaxation of \(z=xy\) over \(B\). Then \[M(B')\subseteq M(B)\cap(B'\times\mathbb R).\] Hence valid domain tightening cannot weaken the relaxation on the retained domain. If the tighter domain excludes an intended feasible factor pair, outer-relaxation validity is lost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tighter valid factor bounds strengthen or preserve a McCormick relaxation, whereas invalid bounds can remove intended feasible points.
assumptions_latex: \(B'\subseteq B\) are finite boxes.
Every intended factor pair retained by the model lies in \(B'\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(B')\subseteq M(B)\cap(B'\times\mathbb R)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonic Strengthening by Valid Domain Tightening

children.title: Reformulation-Induced Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Redundant symmetric lifted representations that impede search or linear algebra.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact restriction of an invariant lift to representatives of its feasible symmetry orbits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a group \(\Gamma\) act on a lifted feasible set \(L\), and suppose the objective \(F\) and projection \(P\) are invariant: \(F(\gamma z)=F(z)\) and \(P(\gamma z)=P(z)\) for all \(z\in L\) and \(\gamma\in\Gamma\). If a set \(B\) intersects every feasible orbit \(\Gamma z\), then \[P(L\cap B)=P(L),\qquad \inf_{z\in L\cap B}F(z)=\inf_{z\in L}F(z).\] Without orbit coverage, these equalities are not guaranteed. Orbit coverage is therefore the exactness condition for this symmetry-breaking restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetry-breaking restriction preserves projection and optimal value when it contains a representative of every invariant feasible orbit.
assumptions_latex: \(\Gamma\) acts on the lifted feasible set \(L\).
The objective and original-variable projection are invariant under the action.
The restriction set \(B\) intersects every feasible orbit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Restricting the lift to \(L\cap B\) preserves its projection and infimum.

notation.meaning: Symmetry group acting on lifted variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Orbit-Preserving Symmetry Breaking

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Change-of-Basis Symmetry in Low-Rank Factor Lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous nonuniqueness introduced by representing a matrix with two low-rank factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times r}\), \(V\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times r}\), and every \(R\in\mathrm{GL}(r)\), \[(UR)(VR^{-\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T}=UV^{\mathsf T}.\] Hence a formulation depending on \((U,V)\) only through \(UV^{\mathsf T}\) contains the full \(\mathrm{GL}(r)\)-orbit of each factor pair. For \(r=1\), this includes \((u,v)\mapsto(\alpha u,\alpha^{-1}v)\) for \(\alpha\ne0\); when both factors are nonzero, their norms can become arbitrarily unbalanced while the represented matrix remains unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A low-rank factor lift is invariant under inverse changes of basis, creating continuous families of equivalent and potentially arbitrarily unbalanced factor coordinates.
assumptions_latex: The lifted model uses \(U\) and \(V\) only through \(UV^{\mathsf T}\).
\(R\) is invertible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each represented matrix has a change-of-basis orbit of equivalent factor pairs, so factor coordinates need not be identifiable or balanced.

notation.meaning: Group of invertible real r-by-r matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Change-of-Basis Symmetry in Low-Rank Factor Lifts

assumptions_latex: Let \(m\ge 2\), let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, and let \(C\subseteq E\) be convex.
Let \(f:E\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and twice differentiable on an open set containing \(C\).
The lifted formulation is \(\min\{f(\sum_{i=1}^m z_i):\sum_{i=1}^m z_i\in C\}\) over \((z_1,\ldots,z_m)\in E^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lifted formulation is invariant under every permutation \(\pi\in S_m\), since replacing \((z_1,\ldots,z_m)\) by \((z_{\pi(1)},\ldots,z_{\pi(m)})\) preserves their sum. More strongly, every perturbation \(d=(d_1,\ldots,d_m)\in E^m\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^m d_i=0\) leaves the represented point unchanged. Hence feasible lifted points occur in redundant affine families of dimension at least \((m-1)\dim E\). The lifted objective Hessian annihilates these directions: \[\nabla^2(f\circ A)(z)d=A^*\nabla^2 f(Az)Ad=0,\qquad A(z)=\sum_{i=1}^m z_i.\] Thus, without symmetry removal, normalization, or regularization, second-order linear systems can be singular despite a well-posed original formulation.

notation.meaning: Permutation group acting on the lifted component indices.
Aggregation map from lifted variables to the represented variable.
Adjoint of the aggregation map under chosen Euclidean inner products.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: duplicated-variable lifts exhibit permutation and nullspace symmetry by direct aggregation-map calculation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete duplicated-variable lift showing how reformulation symmetry creates redundant orbits and singular curvature directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\ge 2\) and define \(A:E^m\to E\) by \(A(z_1,\ldots,z_m)=\sum_{i=1}^m z_i\). Consider the lift of \(\min_{x\in C}f(x)\) obtained by minimizing \(f(Az)\) subject to \(Az\in C\). Every permutation in \(S_m\) preserves the lifted objective and feasible set. Moreover, if \(d\in E^m\) satisfies \(Ad=0\), then \(z+td\) represents the same original point for every \(t\in\mathbb{R}\). Consequently, the lift contains redundant affine families, and \(\nabla^2(f\circ A)(z)d=0\) whenever \(Ad=0\). Thus the reformulation introduces null directions and potentially singular second-order systems that are absent from the original variable space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicating a variable into interchangeable components creates permutation symmetry and zero-sum null directions, producing equivalent lifted points and potentially singular second-order linear systems.
knowledge_statements.title: Reformulation-Induced Symmetry
